levels.title: Software Engineering Fundamentals
levels.scope: Become comfortable building, debugging, and deploying real software before adding LLMs. This is the engineering foundation for everything that follows.

modules.title: Python for AI Engineering

topics.label: Clean, idiomatic Python
topics.detail: Write clean, idiomatic Python using functions, classes, modules, comprehensions, exceptions, and common standard-library utilities.

topics.label: Core data structures
topics.detail: Reason confidently about core data structures: lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, iterators, generators, and when to use each.

topics.label: Type hints & typed models
topics.detail: Use type hints, dataclass/Pydantic-style models, and static analysis to make interfaces explicit and catch mistakes earlier.

topics.label: Mutability, scope & failure modes
topics.detail: Understand mutability, references, scope, exceptions, context managers, and common Python failure modes.

topics.label: Files, paths, env vars & serialization
topics.detail: Work with files, paths, environment variables, JSON, CSV, and basic serialization.

topics.label: Sync vs async execution
topics.detail: Understand synchronous vs asynchronous execution; use async / await to perform concurrent network/API calls without blocking.

topics.label: Environments & dependencies with uv
topics.detail: Manage virtual environments and dependencies with uv; understand pyproject.toml, dependency locking, and reproducible environments.

topics.label: Modules & packages
topics.detail: Structure larger programs into modules and packages instead of writing everything in one script.

topics.label: Unit tests and debugging
topics.detail: Write basic unit tests with pytest and learn to debug using stack traces, logs, and breakpoints.

modules.outcome: Build a small multi-file Python application that is typed, tested, dependency-managed, and capable of making concurrent external API calls.

modules.title: The Web: HTTP, REST & JSON

topics.label: The HTTP request/response cycle
topics.detail: Understand the full HTTP request/response cycle: URL, method, headers, body, server processing, response, and status code.

topics.label: Methods & idempotency
topics.detail: Work with common methods such as GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, and DELETE, and understand idempotency at a practical level.

topics.label: Status codes
topics.detail: Understand important status-code families and common codes such as 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, and 500.

topics.label: Headers, params, bodies & cookies
topics.detail: Understand headers, query parameters, path parameters, request bodies, content types, and cookies at a practical level.

topics.label: Working with JSON
topics.detail: Produce, parse, validate, and manipulate JSON confidently.

topics.label: RESTful resource design
topics.detail: Understand RESTful resource design and design clean endpoints for a simple application.

topics.label: Authentication basics
topics.detail: Understand authentication basics: API keys, bearer tokens, authorization headers, and why secrets should not be embedded in URLs or client code.

topics.label: Inspecting APIs with curl & Postman
topics.detail: Use tools such as curl, Postman/Bruno, or Python HTTP clients to inspect and debug APIs.

modules.outcome: Read unfamiliar API documentation, construct requests manually, interpret responses, and design a sensible REST API.

modules.title: Building APIs with FastAPI

topics.label: Routes, parameters & response models
topics.detail: Build a FastAPI application with routes, path/query parameters, request bodies, and response models.

topics.label: Validation with Pydantic
topics.detail: Use Pydantic models for validation, serialization, typed inputs, and typed outputs.

topics.label: Dependency injection
topics.detail: Understand dependency injection at a practical level for reusable application dependencies.

topics.label: Status codes & error responses
topics.detail: Return appropriate HTTP status codes and design consistent error responses.

topics.label: Clean exception handling
topics.detail: Handle exceptions cleanly instead of leaking raw stack traces to clients.

topics.label: Generated OpenAPI docs
topics.detail: Use FastAPI's automatically generated OpenAPI/Swagger documentation and understand how API schemas are derived.

topics.label: Sync vs async endpoints
topics.detail: Write synchronous and asynchronous endpoints and understand when each is appropriate.

topics.label: Calling external services without blocking
topics.detail: Call external HTTP services from async endpoints without blocking the server.

topics.label: Startup, config & middleware
topics.detail: Understand application startup/shutdown, configuration through environment variables, and basic middleware concepts.

topics.label: Testing endpoints
topics.detail: Test endpoints using pytest and FastAPI's test client.

modules.outcome: Build a documented, validated, testable API that communicates with at least one external service.

modules.title: Data & Persistence Basics

topics.label: Relational data modeling
topics.detail: Understand relational data modeling: tables, rows, columns, primary keys, foreign keys, relationships, and basic normalization.

topics.label: SQL with PostgreSQL
topics.detail: Use PostgreSQL and write SQL for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, filtering, sorting, grouping, joins, and basic aggregations.

topics.label: Indexes & query performance
topics.detail: Understand indexes conceptually and why query design affects performance.

topics.label: Connecting a database to the app
topics.detail: Connect PostgreSQL to a Python/FastAPI application using a database driver or ORM.

topics.label: Credentials outside source code
topics.detail: Keep database credentials outside source code and manage configuration through environment variables.

modules.outcome: Build an API whose data survives application restarts and supports real CRUD operations backed by PostgreSQL.

modules.title: Git & Collaboration

topics.label: Repos, commits, branches & remotes
topics.detail: Understand repositories, commits, branches, remotes, diffs, and the staging area.

topics.label: The branch → PR → merge workflow
topics.detail: Follow a practical workflow: branch → make changes → commit → push → pull request → review → merge.

topics.label: Commit messages & history
topics.detail: Write useful commit messages and inspect history using Git tools.

topics.label: Resolving merge conflicts
topics.detail: Resolve merge conflicts confidently rather than avoiding them.

topics.label: Keeping secrets out with .gitignore
topics.detail: Understand .gitignore and prevent secrets, virtual environments, generated files, and local configuration from entering the repository.

topics.label: Writing a README
topics.detail: Write a README that explains what the project does, how to install it, configure it, run it, test it, and call its API.

topics.label: Code review & protected branches
topics.detail: Understand basic collaboration concepts such as code review, pull requests, and protected main branches.

modules.outcome: Hand another developer your repository and have them understand, run, and contribute to it without needing you beside them.

modules.title: AI-Assisted Software Development

topics.label: Autocomplete → assistants → agents
topics.detail: Understand the progression from autocomplete, to chat-based assistants, to coding agents that can read a repository, edit code, run commands, inspect the results, and iterate.

topics.label: AI-assisted engineering vs vibe coding
topics.detail: Distinguish AI-assisted engineering, where you direct and verify the work, from blind vibe coding, where you accept whatever is generated.

topics.label: Explore, implement & debug with an agent
topics.detail: Use a coding agent such as Claude Code to explore an unfamiliar repository, implement targeted changes, and debug existing code.

topics.label: The verification loop
topics.detail: Work the verification loop on every change: give context → generate → inspect the Git diff → test → debug → review → accept.

topics.label: Minimum useful context
topics.detail: Understand the finite context window and give the minimum useful context for a task instead of pointing the agent at the entire repository.

topics.label: CLAUDE.md as project memory
topics.detail: Keep architecture, conventions, project commands, and testing instructions in a project instruction file such as CLAUDE.md, separate from temporary task context.

topics.label: Spec-driven development & planning
topics.detail: Practice spec-driven development: write the requirement and the specification, then review a plan before the agent changes the repository.

topics.label: Slash commands & Skills
topics.detail: Turn prompts you retype into custom slash commands, and understand Skills as reusable capabilities with instructions, metadata, and examples that load only when needed.

topics.label: Skills worth building
topics.detail: Build skills for recurring work such as code review, test generation, documentation, refactoring, and repository-specific conventions.

topics.label: Delegating to subagents
topics.detail: Delegate specialized work to subagents such as a reviewer, tester, debugger, or researcher instead of forcing every responsibility into one context.

topics.label: External systems through MCP
topics.detail: Connect the agent to systems outside the repository through MCP (Model Context Protocol): databases, APIs, developer tools, and documentation.

topics.label: Hooks for deterministic checks
topics.detail: Use hooks to make formatting, linting, testing, and validation deterministic instead of asking a model to remember them.

topics.label: Plugins as capability bundles
topics.detail: Understand plugins as reusable bundles that package commands, skills, hooks, agents, and integrations together.

topics.label: Skills that transfer across agents
topics.detail: Understand that these skills transfer to any coding agent — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI — because the durable parts are context, specifications, planning, delegation, automation, and verification.

modules.outcome: Use a coding agent as an engineering collaborator across exploration, implementation, debugging, refactoring, and testing, with planning and verification around every meaningful change.

modules.title: Containers & Deployment

topics.label: App vs environment vs machine
topics.detail: Understand the practical distinction between your application, its environment, and the machine running it.

topics.label: Containers & images
topics.detail: Understand containers and images conceptually and why Docker improves reproducibility.

topics.label: Writing and running a Dockerfile
topics.detail: Write a Dockerfile, build an image, run a container locally, expose ports, and pass environment variables safely.

topics.label: Layers, logs & startup failures
topics.detail: Understand image layers, .dockerignore, container logs, and common container startup failures.

topics.label: Containerizing a FastAPI app
topics.detail: Containerize a FastAPI application and connect it to its required configuration/services.

topics.label: Deploying to a public URL
topics.detail: Deploy a service to a cloud/platform provider and expose it through a publicly reachable URL.

topics.label: Production env vars & secrets
topics.detail: Configure production environment variables and secrets separately from local development.

modules.outcome: Take a service that works locally, containerize it, deploy it, and debug it when the production environment behaves differently.

modules.title: Capstone: Ship a No-AI REST Service

projects.title: Capstone: Ship a No-AI REST Service
projects.result: a real service that another person can clone, run, test, call over HTTP, and inspect without any AI component hiding weak software-engineering fundamentals.

checklist.label: The full no-AI stack
checklist.detail: Build a complete application using Python + FastAPI + PostgreSQL + Git + Docker + deployment, with no LLM or AI dependency.

checklist.label: Choosing a realistic domain
checklist.detail: Design a small but realistic domain such as task management, bookmarks, expense tracking, inventory, notes, or support tickets.

checklist.label: REST endpoints with persistent CRUD
checklist.detail: Implement multiple REST endpoints with validated request/response schemas and persistent CRUD operations.

checklist.label: An external API integration
checklist.detail: Include at least one external API integration and use async execution where appropriate.

checklist.label: Handling every failure path
checklist.detail: Handle validation failures, missing resources, external-service errors, and unexpected server errors cleanly.

checklist.label: Tests, config & logging
checklist.detail: Add basic automated tests, configuration via environment variables, and useful application logging.

checklist.label: Clean repo and README
checklist.detail: Maintain the project in Git with a clean repository structure and a README containing setup and usage instructions.

checklist.label: Docker packaging & deployment
checklist.detail: Package the service with Docker and deploy it to a publicly reachable URL.

checklist.label: Verifying the deployed API
checklist.detail: Verify the deployed API using its OpenAPI docs, curl, or an API client.

checklist.label: Coding agent during the build
checklist.detail: Use a coding agent for meaningful parts of the build; "no-AI" means the deployed product needs no LLM, not that you code without AI tools.

checklist.label: Diff review before accepting
checklist.detail: Review every meaningful generated change through its Git diff before accepting it.

checklist.label: Validating generated code
checklist.detail: Validate generated code through tests, type checking, linting, logs, and manual API calls.

checklist.label: Explain it without the agent
checklist.detail: Explain the architecture and the important code paths yourself, without asking the coding agent.

checklist.label: Document one AI failure
checklist.detail: Document one case where the coding agent produced an incorrect, incomplete, insecure, over-engineered, or otherwise suboptimal solution: what it proposed, why it was wrong, how you detected it, what you changed, and the engineering lesson you took from it.

levels.title: LLM 101
levels.scope: Build a strong mental model of how LLMs work, why they behave the way they do, and how to choose and use the right model for a task.

modules.title: What an LLM Actually Is

topics.label: Next-token prediction
topics.detail: Understand what a Large Language Model actually does, with next-token prediction as the core idea and generation as a repeated predict → choose → append → repeat process.

topics.label: What an LLM is not
topics.detail: Understand what an LLM is not: a database, search engine, deterministic program, or repository of stored answers.

topics.label: Why one model does many tasks
topics.detail: Understand why the same underlying model can perform writing, summarization, translation, coding, question answering, and classification.

topics.label: Where capability comes from
topics.detail: Build intuition for how capability improves through better data, more compute, larger models, and better training.

modules.outcome: Explain an LLM simply: an LLM generates text by repeatedly predicting the most appropriate next token given the tokens it has already seen.

modules.title: Tokenization

topics.label: Characters, words & tokens
topics.detail: Distinguish characters, words, and tokens; understand token IDs, why LLMs operate on tokens, and why different tokenizers can split the same text differently.

topics.label: Tokenizing across languages & code
topics.detail: Explore tokenization of normal English, uncommon words, numbers, code, emojis, Hindi/Devanagari, and mixed Hindi-English text.

topics.label: Why tokens drive cost and latency
topics.detail: Connect tokenization to API pricing, context-window consumption, output length, latency, spelling difficulties, character-counting failures, and mathematical/numerical behavior.

modules.outcome: Explain why two texts with roughly the same number of words can have very different token counts and LLM costs.

modules.title: Inside an LLM: Embeddings, Attention & Transformers

topics.label: From token IDs to embeddings
topics.detail: Understand how token IDs become embeddings, what vectors represent conceptually, why concepts are represented numerically, and how representations change as they pass through transformer layers.

topics.label: What parameter counts mean
topics.detail: Understand what model parameters are and what sizes such as 8B, 70B, and 400B+ mean.

topics.label: Why bigger is not automatically better
topics.detail: Understand why more parameters can increase capacity, while larger does not automatically mean better.

topics.label: The intuition behind attention
topics.detail: Understand attention through the intuition: a token looks at other relevant tokens in the context to build a better representation of what it means.

topics.label: Queries, keys, values & causal attention
topics.detail: Build a high-level understanding of queries, keys, values, attention scores, transformer layers, and causal attention — without matrix mathematics.

topics.label: Dense models
topics.detail: Understand a dense model, where every parameter takes part in producing every token.

topics.label: Mixture-of-Experts & routing
topics.detail: Understand a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, where the feed-forward layers are split into many experts and a router selects only a few of them for each token.

topics.label: Total vs active parameters
topics.detail: Distinguish total parameters from active parameters, and understand why an MoE model with a very large total size can cost far less to run than a dense model of the same size.

topics.label: What MoE changes in practice
topics.detail: Understand what MoE changes in practice: every expert still has to be held in memory, while the compute spent per token stays closer to that of a much smaller model.

topics.label: Reading MoE model cards
topics.detail: Read MoE descriptions on model cards, such as "8x7B" or "total vs active parameters", and know what they tell you about speed, cost, and hosting requirements.

modules.outcome: Explain conceptually what happens between a token entering the model and the model producing next-token probabilities.

modules.title: How LLMs Learn

topics.label: Pretraining & self-supervision
topics.detail: Understand pretraining, how enormous text datasets are used, why next-token prediction creates its own training signal, and what self-supervised learning means.

topics.label: What pretraining teaches
topics.detail: Understand how pretraining enables models to learn grammar, facts, patterns, concepts, relationships, coding syntax, and problem-solving patterns.

topics.label: Memorization vs generalization
topics.detail: Explore memorization vs generalization, including why an LLM can sometimes answer questions it has never seen verbatim.

topics.label: The post-training pipeline
topics.detail: Understand the broad pipeline: Pretraining → Supervised Fine-Tuning → Preference / Reinforcement Training → Deployed Assistant.

topics.label: SFT, RLHF & preference optimization
topics.detail: Understand SFT, RLHF, RLAIF, preference optimization at a conceptual level, and safety tuning.

topics.label: Why chat models behave as they do
topics.detail: Connect post-training to why chat models follow instructions, answer conversationally, refuse certain requests, hedge, structure answers, and ask for clarification.

modules.outcome: Explain why a pretrained model may know a lot while still being a poor conversational assistant.

modules.title: How LLM Inference Works

topics.label: What happens after you send a prompt
topics.detail: Understand what happens after sending a prompt to an LLM API: Prompt → process input → predict token → generate token → repeat.

topics.label: Prefill vs decode
topics.detail: Distinguish prefill, where the model processes the input/context, from decode, where new tokens are generated one by one.

topics.label: Tokens, TTFT & total latency
topics.detail: Understand input tokens, output tokens, time to first token (TTFT), tokens per second, and total latency.

topics.label: KV caching
topics.detail: Build intuition for KV caching and why the model does not need to recompute the entire conversation from scratch after every generated token.

topics.label: Why inference mechanics drive cost
topics.detail: Connect inference mechanics to latency, cost, long prompts, long outputs, and reasoning models.

modules.outcome: Explain why generating 2,000 output tokens usually takes much longer than generating 50 tokens even with the same input.

modules.title: Sampling & Generation Parameters

topics.label: From probabilities to a chosen token
topics.detail: Start from the model's next-token probability distribution and ask: which token should actually be generated?

topics.label: Temperature, top-p, top-k & penalties
topics.detail: Understand greedy decoding, temperature, top-p, top-k, maximum output tokens, stop sequences, and repetition/frequency/presence penalties where supported.

topics.label: Matching randomness to the task
topics.detail: Understand task-dependent randomness: lower randomness for extraction, structured output, classification, and factual QA; higher randomness for brainstorming, creative writing, and diverse alternatives.

topics.label: Differences across model APIs
topics.detail: Understand that different model APIs expose different controls and that some reasoning models provide less direct control over traditional sampling parameters.

modules.outcome: Choose sensible generation settings based on the task instead of changing temperature arbitrarily.

modules.title: Reasoning Models & Test-Time Compute

topics.label: Why some models think longer
topics.detail: Understand why some models spend substantially more compute before producing an answer.

topics.label: Test-time compute & thinking budgets
topics.detail: Build intuition for test-time compute, reasoning effort, thinking budgets, and internal reasoning tokens/compute.

topics.label: Where reasoning helps
topics.detail: Identify tasks where reasoning tends to help: difficult mathematics, complex coding, planning, multi-step logic, and constraint-heavy problems.

topics.label: Where reasoning is unnecessary
topics.detail: Identify tasks where it may be unnecessary: sentiment classification, simple extraction, rewriting, and straightforward summarization.

topics.label: The quality / cost / latency trade-off
topics.detail: Understand the trade-off: more reasoning can improve quality but generally increases cost and latency.

topics.label: Prompting reasoning models
topics.detail: Adapt prompting for reasoning models: move away from relying on “think step by step” and instead clearly state the goal, provide relevant context, specify constraints, and define what a good answer looks like.

modules.outcome: Recognize when paying for extra reasoning compute is likely to be worthwhile.

modules.title: The Context Window

topics.label: What occupies the context window
topics.detail: Understand what the context window is and what can occupy it: system instructions, conversation history, user prompts, documents, examples, tool outputs, and generated content.

topics.label: Context ≠ knowledge ≠ memory
topics.detail: Distinguish context ≠ model knowledge ≠ long-term memory.

topics.label: What goes wrong in long contexts
topics.detail: Understand what can happen with very long contexts: truncation, attention degradation, lost-in-the-middle effects, and context dilution.

topics.label: Why a big window is not enough
topics.detail: Understand why a model supporting a huge context window does not mean it can use every token equally well.

modules.outcome: Decide whether a task needs a larger-context model or a better strategy for selecting what enters context.

modules.title: LLM Capabilities & Failure Modes

topics.label: Common strengths
topics.detail: Understand common strengths: summarization, text transformation, extraction, classification, semantic understanding, coding, translation, brainstorming, working with unstructured information, and few-shot adaptation.

topics.label: Common failure modes
topics.detail: Understand common failure modes: hallucination, arithmetic mistakes, brittle reasoning, instruction-following failures, prompt sensitivity, context failures, outdated knowledge, nondeterminism, and confident incorrect answers.

topics.label: Why hallucination happens
topics.detail: Understand hallucination mechanistically: an LLM is trained to generate a likely continuation, not to independently verify that every generated statement is true, which makes fluent incorrect answers possible.

topics.label: Asking "how reliably?" instead of "can it?"
topics.detail: Adopt the engineering question: instead of “Can GPT do this?”, ask “How reliably does this model perform this task under the conditions of my application?”

modules.outcome: Predict which tasks are naturally well suited to LLMs and which require additional safeguards.

modules.title: Understanding the Model Landscape

topics.label: Closed and API models
topics.detail: Understand closed/API models through trade-offs involving frontier capability, convenience, infrastructure, privacy, vendor dependence, and control.

topics.label: Open-weight models
topics.detail: Understand open-weight models through self-hosting, privacy, customization, infrastructure requirements, and operational complexity.

topics.label: Managed platforms & hosted open weights
topics.detail: Understand the third path between them: managed platforms such as AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Azure AI Foundry serve both closed and open-weight models inside your own cloud account, and inference providers host open weights for you without any hardware of your own.

topics.label: Other useful distinctions
topics.detail: Learn other useful distinctions: small vs large, dense vs Mixture-of-Experts, general-purpose vs specialized, reasoning vs non-reasoning, and text-only vs multimodal.

topics.label: There is no universally best LLM
topics.detail: Internalize the core principle: there is no universally best LLM; the best model depends on the workload.

topics.label: Knowledge cutoffs
topics.detail: Understand that a model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff, and that anything newer has to arrive through context, retrieval, or tools.

topics.label: Versions, snapshots & deprecations
topics.detail: Track model versions and dated snapshots, and expect deprecations: the model behind a familiar name can change or be retired, so pin a version and re-test when it moves.

topics.label: Open-weight licensing
topics.detail: Check the license before building on an open-weight model, since permissive, restricted-use, and non-commercial terms differ in what you are allowed to ship.

modules.outcome: Compare two models using meaningful architectural, capability, and deployment differences rather than relying purely on leaderboard rank.

modules.title: Benchmarks & Leaderboards

topics.label: What a benchmark is
topics.detail: Understand what a benchmark is: a fixed set of tasks with a fixed scoring method, used to measure different models against the same yardstick.

topics.label: Benchmarks quoted on model cards
topics.detail: Recognize the benchmarks quoted on model cards — knowledge and reasoning tests such as MMLU and GPQA, coding tests, and mathematics tests — and know roughly what each one measures.

topics.label: Kinds of leaderboard
topics.detail: Read the main kinds of leaderboard: human-preference rankings such as LMArena/Chatbot Arena, aggregated capability/cost/latency dashboards, and open-model leaderboards.

topics.label: Why rank does not transfer
topics.detail: Understand why a leaderboard rank rarely transfers to your application: different prompts, different tasks, averaged scores, and someone else's definition of a good answer.

topics.label: What inflates published scores
topics.detail: Understand the pitfalls that inflate published scores: data contamination, saturated benchmarks, overfitting to public test sets, and favorable run configurations.

topics.label: From leaderboard to shortlist
topics.detail: Use benchmarks and leaderboards for the one thing they do well — narrowing a crowded field to a shortlist — and then judge the shortlist on your own examples.

modules.outcome: Read benchmark tables and leaderboards without being misled by them, and turn them into a shortlist rather than a decision.

modules.title: Choosing the Right Model

topics.label: Eight dimensions for model choice
topics.detail: Evaluate models across eight dimensions:

topics.label: Capability
topics.detail: Capability: Can it perform the task at all?

topics.label: Quality
topics.detail: Quality: How reliably does it perform your specific task?

topics.label: Latency
topics.detail: Latency: How quickly does it respond?

topics.label: Cost
topics.detail: Cost: What will each request cost at your expected usage?

topics.label: Context
topics.detail: Context: Can it accommodate the required input?

topics.label: Modalities
topics.detail: Modalities: Do you need text, images, audio, or video?

topics.label: Privacy & deployment
topics.detail: Privacy & deployment: Can you use an external API, do you need a managed platform inside your own cloud, or do you require self-hosting?

topics.label: Product features
topics.detail: Product features: Do you require structured outputs, function calling, tools, streaming, or caching?

topics.label: Reading model cards & pricing pages
topics.detail: Learn to critically read model cards, benchmark tables, pricing pages, context-window specifications, and API documentation.

topics.label: Why benchmarks alone are not enough
topics.detail: Understand why benchmark scores alone should not determine model selection.

topics.label: The selection workflow
topics.detail: Follow the workflow: Define task → Identify requirements → Shortlist models → Test on your own examples → Measure quality → Measure latency → Measure cost → Inspect failures → Choose the model.

modules.outcome: Select models based on application requirements and empirical performance rather than popularity or leaderboard position.

levels.title: Working with LLM APIs (Orchestration)
levels.scope: Turn individual LLM calls into reliable software workflows — messages, streaming, structured outputs, tools, multi-step orchestration, concurrency, failure handling, and observability. RAG and agents come later.

topics.label: Messages, roles & usage metadata
topics.detail: Call OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs; work with models, messages, system instructions, user/assistant roles, response objects, stop reasons, and usage metadata.

topics.label: APIs are stateless
topics.detail: Understand that most LLM APIs are fundamentally stateless and learn to maintain conversation history explicitly.

topics.label: Application state vs model context
topics.detail: Distinguish application state from information currently present in the model's context.

topics.label: Managing API keys safely
topics.detail: Manage API keys safely using environment variables, .env files, or secret managers; never expose server-side credentials in frontend code.

topics.label: Inspecting the full response object
topics.detail: Inspect input/output tokens, request metadata, and model responses instead of treating the API as a simple prompt → string function.

topics.label: Rendering output incrementally
topics.detail: Stream model output incrementally and render partial responses in a terminal or UI.

topics.label: TTFT & perceived latency
topics.detail: Understand TTFT, generation speed, perceived latency, and total latency.

topics.label: Accumulating and interrupting streams
topics.detail: Accumulate streamed events into a complete response and handle cancellations, interrupted streams, network failures, and incomplete generations.

topics.label: Why orchestration libraries exist
topics.detail: Understand why orchestration libraries exist and what LangChain abstracts over raw provider SDKs.

topics.label: Models, templates & output parsers
topics.detail: Work with chat models, messages, prompt templates, output parsers, streaming, and model configuration.

topics.label: Working across providers
topics.detail: Use LangChain with multiple model providers while understanding the underlying API calls it is making.

topics.label: Composing pipelines with runnables
topics.detail: Learn the core composition model and build simple pipelines using prompts, models, parsers, and runnables.

topics.label: Raw SDK vs LangChain
topics.detail: Compare equivalent implementations using raw SDKs and LangChain to understand convenience vs abstraction overhead.

topics.label: LangChain is a layer, not the model
topics.detail: Keep the mental model that LangChain is an orchestration layer, not the LLM itself.

topics.label: Schema-constrained generation
topics.detail: Generate schema-constrained outputs rather than relying on “please return JSON” prompting.

topics.label: Defining schemas
topics.detail: Define schemas using JSON Schema/Pydantic; work with required fields, optional fields, enums, lists, nested objects, and typed responses.

topics.label: Provider-native vs framework support
topics.detail: Implement structured outputs using both provider-native capabilities and LangChain abstractions.

topics.label: Validating before use
topics.detail: Validate model outputs before passing them into application logic.

topics.label: Syntactic validity vs semantic correctness
topics.detail: Distinguish syntactic validity from semantic correctness: valid JSON can still contain incorrect information.

topics.label: Generate → validate → repair
topics.detail: Implement a generate → validate → accept / retry / repair / reject workflow for invalid outputs.

topics.label: Who chooses and who executes
topics.detail: Understand that the LLM normally chooses a tool and generates arguments; your application executes the actual function.

topics.label: Defining a tool
topics.detail: Define tools using names, descriptions, parameter schemas, types, and required arguments.

topics.label: The full tool-calling loop

topics.label: Tool-call IDs & returning results

topics.label: Provider APIs vs LangChain tools

topics.label: Sequential, repeated & parallel calls

topics.label: Tool failures & malformed arguments
topics.detail: Handle tool failures and malformed arguments instead of assuming every requested invocation is executable.

topics.label: Names, descriptions & types
topics.detail: Design tools with precise names, clear descriptions, minimal parameters, strong types, and useful error responses.

topics.label: Ambiguous & overlapping tools
topics.detail: Understand how ambiguous or overlapping tools can cause incorrect tool selection.

topics.label: Too many undifferentiated tools
topics.detail: Avoid giving the model huge numbers of poorly differentiated tools or unnecessary arguments.

topics.label: Treating arguments as untrusted
topics.detail: Treat model-generated arguments as untrusted input: validate types, values, permissions, and potentially destructive operations before execution.

topics.label: Tool descriptions are context
topics.detail: Understand that tool descriptions themselves are part of the context the model uses to decide what action to take.

topics.label: Beyond prompt → model → answer
topics.detail: Move beyond prompt → model → answer and build workflows containing multiple LLM calls, tools, transformations, and application logic.

topics.label: Sequential, routed & fan-out patterns
topics.detail: Implement common orchestration patterns: sequential pipelines, routing, conditional branches, and fan-out/fan-in.

topics.label: When to split a task
topics.detail: Learn when to split a complex task into multiple specialized calls instead of using one enormous prompt.

topics.label: Building by hand, then composing
topics.detail: Build some workflows manually to understand their control flow, then reproduce them using LangChain composition primitives.

topics.label: Workflows vs agents

topics.label: When concurrency helps
topics.detail: Understand synchronous vs asynchronous API calls and when concurrency improves throughput.

topics.label: Running requests concurrently
topics.detail: Process many independent LLM requests concurrently rather than sequentially.

topics.label: Bounded concurrency & rate limits
topics.detail: Use bounded concurrency so higher throughput does not immediately create rate-limit failures.

topics.label: Async and batch execution
topics.detail: Apply async and batch execution using both provider SDKs and orchestration-layer abstractions.

topics.label: The throughput / cost trade-off
topics.detail: Understand the trade-off between concurrency, throughput, latency, API limits, resource consumption, and cost.

topics.label: Common API failures
topics.detail: Recognize common API failures: authentication errors, invalid requests, rate limits, server errors, network failures, timeouts, context-limit errors, and malformed model outputs.

topics.label: What to retry and what to fail fast
topics.detail: Decide which failures should be retried and which should fail immediately; for example, authentication errors generally should not be retried while transient server errors may be.

topics.label: Backoff, jitter, timeouts & degradation
topics.detail: Implement exponential backoff, jitter, maximum retry counts, sensible request timeouts, and graceful degradation.

topics.label: Model and provider fallbacks
topics.detail: Add model/provider fallbacks when appropriate, while understanding that fallback models may differ in quality and behavior.

topics.label: Failures at the LLM and tool levels
topics.detail: Handle failures at both levels: LLM API failure and tool/API failure.

topics.label: Where reliability logic belongs
topics.detail: Understand where reliability logic should live: provider SDK, orchestration layer, or your application code.

topics.label: What to record per request
topics.detail: Track model, input tokens, output tokens, latency, retries, errors, tool calls, and estimated cost for every request.

topics.label: Interactions as traces
topics.detail: Treat a multi-step LLM interaction as a trace rather than an isolated API call.

topics.label: Finding the failing step
topics.detail: Inspect which step caused a failure, which call consumed the most tokens, which tool was selected, and where latency accumulated.

topics.label: Tracing a full workflow
topics.detail: Use callbacks/tracing to understand LangChain workflows and connect individual model and tool calls into a single execution trace.

topics.label: Logging you can actually debug with
topics.detail: Build enough logging and tracing that you can debug workflows without relying on scattered print() statements.

topics.label: LangChain is one approach among many
topics.detail: Understand that LangChain is one orchestration approach rather than a universal standard.

topics.label: LlamaIndex
topics.detail: Explore LlamaIndex and how its abstractions and emphasis differ from LangChain.

topics.label: Graph & state-machine orchestration
topics.detail: Explore graph/state-machine style orchestration for workflows containing branches, loops, persistent state, and more complex control flow.

topics.label: LangGraph
topics.detail: Get introduced to LangGraph as a graph-based approach for stateful LLM workflows.

topics.label: DSPy
topics.detail: Get introduced to DSPy as a more declarative approach where you specify desired input/output behavior rather than manually composing every prompt.

topics.label: Comparing orchestration approaches
topics.detail: Compare orchestration approaches on development speed, abstraction overhead, debugging, portability, dependency complexity, state management, and control.

topics.label: Choosing one for your application
topics.detail: Develop the ability to choose between raw SDKs, LangChain, graph-based frameworks, LlamaIndex, DSPy, or a custom orchestration layer based on the application.

checklist.label: A streaming assistant with real tools
checklist.detail: Build a conversational assistant that maintains history, uses system instructions, streams responses, and exposes at least 2–3 real tools/APIs.

checklist.label: Sequential or parallel tool use
checklist.detail: Support sequential or parallel tool use where appropriate and validate all model-generated tool arguments.

checklist.detail: Add structured outputs where useful, retry transient failures, enforce timeouts, and handle tool/API errors gracefully.

checklist.detail: Record token usage, latency, retries, tool calls, and estimated cost so the entire workflow can be inspected.

checklist.detail: Build the main implementation using LangChain while being able to explain the raw API/tool-call mechanics underneath it.

checklist.label: LLM + software + tools + reliability
checklist.detail: The final application should combine LLM + software + external tools + control flow + reliability, without relying on RAG or autonomous agents.

levels.title: Prompt Engineering

topics.detail: Use system/user/assistant roles correctly and understand instruction priority.

topics.detail: Separate instructions clearly from user-provided or external data.

topics.detail: Distinguish few-shot prompting from fine-tuning.

topics.label: When reasoning is unnecessary

topics.label: Prompting reasoning models

topics.label: Stable rules vs task instructions
topics.detail: Separate stable application rules from task-specific user instructions.

topics.label: Handling missing or out-of-scope input
topics.detail: Specify what the model should do when information is missing, ambiguous, or outside scope.

topics.label: Lightweight behavioural guardrails
topics.detail: Add lightweight behavioral guardrails without turning the system prompt into an enormous rulebook.

topics.label: Controlling style, length & format
topics.detail: Control response style, length, format, headings, labels, tables, and JSON through clear instructions and examples.

topics.label: When prompting is not enough
topics.detail: Know when prompting is enough and when structured-output/schema enforcement from Level 2 is more reliable.

topics.label: Semantic instruction vs format enforcement
topics.detail: Separate semantic instructions from programmatic format enforcement.

topics.label: Diagnosing prompt failures
topics.detail: Diagnose failures caused by ambiguous instructions, conflicting constraints, poor examples, missing context, or unclear output requirements.

topics.label: Building a small test set
topics.detail: Build a small test set containing normal cases, edge cases, and known failures.

topics.label: Comparing versions on the same examples
topics.detail: Compare prompt versions on the same examples instead of judging them from individual responses.

topics.label: Reducing variance & regressions
topics.detail: Reduce unnecessary output variance and regressions through systematic iteration.

topics.label: Versioning prompts like code
topics.detail: Version prompts like code and track which prompt/model combination produced each result.

topics.label: Comparing on quality, latency & cost
topics.detail: Compare prompt variants using quality, latency, token usage, and cost.

topics.label: Trimming unnecessary context
topics.detail: Remove unnecessary context and repeated instructions.

topics.label: Prompt caching & reusable prefixes
topics.detail: Understand prompt caching and structure reusable prompt prefixes to benefit from caching where supported.

topics.label: What prompt injection is
topics.detail: Understand prompt injection and why external/user-controlled text should be treated as untrusted data.

topics.label: Recognising override attempts
topics.detail: Recognize attempts to override system instructions or extract hidden information.

topics.label: Wording is not a security boundary
topics.detail: Understand that prompt wording alone is not a security boundary; permissions and sensitive actions must be controlled by application code.

topics.label: Deeper defences come later
topics.detail: Leave deeper adversarial security and defenses for the later security level.

checklist.label: Choosing a realistic task

checklist.detail: correctness

checklist.detail: consistency

checklist.detail: token usage

checklist.detail: latency/cost.

checklist.detail: Select the final prompt based on measured performance rather than intuition.

levels.title: RAG
levels.scope: Build the retrieval layer that RAG depends on — ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector search, and hybrid retrieval — then ground LLMs in external knowledge, improve retrieval quality, and learn the major RAG architectures used beyond a naive retrieve-and-generate pipeline.

modules.title: Data ingestion & document processing

topics.label: Extracting from PDFs, HTML & DOCX
topics.detail: Extract content from common sources such as PDFs, HTML, DOCX, and structured documents; understand when OCR is required.

topics.label: Cleaning while keeping structure
topics.detail: Clean and normalize messy text while preserving useful document structure and metadata.

topics.label: Duplicates, updates & re-indexing
topics.detail: Handle duplicate documents, document updates, and incremental re-indexing.

modules.outcome: Convert a real-world document collection into clean, structured data ready for retrieval.

modules.title: Chunking strategies

topics.label: Why documents must be split
topics.detail: Understand why documents must usually be split before embedding and retrieval.

topics.label: Fixed, recursive, structural & semantic
topics.detail: Apply fixed-size, recursive, structural, and semantic chunking.

topics.label: Size, overlap, boundaries & metadata
topics.detail: Reason about chunk size, overlap, boundaries, and metadata and how they affect retrieval quality.

topics.label: Precise chunks vs context-rich chunks

modules.outcome: Choose a sensible chunking strategy based on document structure and query type.

topics.detail: Understand embeddings as vector representations that capture semantic relationships between text.

topics.label: Generating embeddings
topics.detail: Generate embeddings for documents and queries using an embedding model.

topics.label: Choosing an embedding model
topics.detail: Understand dimensions, embedding model choice, multilingual/domain performance, cost, and latency trade-offs.

topics.label: Vector spaces cannot be mixed
topics.detail: Understand that embeddings from different models/vector spaces generally cannot be mixed directly.

modules.outcome: Select and use an embedding model appropriate for a retrieval task.

topics.detail: Understand cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance and how they are used to compare vectors.

topics.detail: Build a simple semantic-search system from scratch: query → embedding → similarity → top-k results.

topics.label: Semantic similarity vs keyword match
topics.detail: Understand the difference between semantic similarity and exact keyword matching.

topics.label: Where semantic search fails

modules.outcome: Build semantic search without relying on a vector database and understand exactly what the database will later automate.

topics.detail: Understand traditional lexical retrieval and BM25, and why keyword search can outperform embeddings for some queries.

topics.label: Sparse vs dense retrieval
topics.detail: Compare sparse/BM25 retrieval with dense/vector retrieval.

topics.detail: Combine dense and sparse results using hybrid retrieval and techniques such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

topics.label: When hybrid retrieval helps
topics.detail: Understand when hybrid retrieval helps, especially for queries containing names, technical terms, IDs, numbers, and exact phrases.

topics.detail: Understand the core pipeline: query → retrieve → assemble context → generate answer.

topics.label: What RAG solves
topics.detail: Understand what RAG solves: private knowledge, frequently changing information, large knowledge bases, and source-grounded answers.

topics.label: When not to use RAG
topics.detail: Know when not to use RAG: when the model already knows enough, the task is purely transformational, or the required knowledge can simply fit in context.

topics.detail: Distinguish retrieval failure from generation failure.

topics.detail: Build a complete RAG pipeline manually using the retrieval system built earlier in this level.

topics.label: Handling weak or missing context
topics.detail: Handle cases where retrieval returns weak, irrelevant, or insufficient context.

topics.detail: Understand the two-stage pattern: retrieve many candidates → rerank → send the best chunks to the LLM.

topics.detail: Understand why the user's original question is not always the best retrieval query.

topics.label: The extra calls it costs

topics.label: When to skip transformation
topics.detail: Avoid query transformation when baseline retrieval already performs well.

topics.detail: Generate answers grounded in retrieved evidence rather than unsupported model knowledge.

topics.detail: Understand that having citations is not the same as being grounded; the cited source must actually support the claim.

topics.detail: Detect insufficient evidence and respond with an appropriate “I don't know / insufficient information” instead of forcing an answer.

topics.detail: Learn Self-RAG: retrieval is performed when needed and the model reflects on retrieved evidence and its generated response.

topics.label: CRAG (Corrective RAG)
topics.detail: Learn CRAG (Corrective RAG): evaluate retrieved evidence and trigger corrective retrieval when the initial results are weak.

topics.label: Adaptive RAG

topics.label: When Graph RAG is useful

topics.detail: Compare advanced approaches on quality, complexity, latency, cost, and failure mode addressed rather than assuming more advanced RAG is always better.

topics.label: Direct vs indirect injection

topics.label: What injection attacks attempt
topics.detail: Understand attacks that attempt to override instructions, manipulate tools, expose private context, or redirect an agent's objective.

topics.label: Untrusted input + tools + an exit path
topics.detail: Understand the dangerous combination of untrusted input + powerful tools/private data + an exfiltration path.

topics.label: Layered defences
topics.detail: Defend using instruction/data separation, least privilege, authorization checks, restricted tools, confirmation gates, and output validation.

topics.label: Why "ignore malicious instructions" fails

modules.outcome: Build applications that remain safe even when malicious instructions reach the model.

modules.title: Agent & tool security

topics.label: Least privilege for agents

topics.label: Read-only vs consequential actions

topics.label: Validating tool use outside the LLM

topics.label: Human approval for irreversible actions
topics.detail: Add human approval for sensitive or irreversible operations.

topics.label: Step, runtime & cost limits
topics.detail: Limit agent steps, runtime, cost, and tool usage to prevent runaway execution.

topics.label: Sandboxing generated code
topics.detail: Sandbox model-generated code and treat generated SQL, commands, URLs, or API calls as untrusted.

modules.outcome: Give agents useful autonomy without giving them unrestricted control over real systems.

modules.title: RAG & knowledge security

topics.label: Retrieved documents are data, not instructions
topics.detail: Treat retrieved documents as untrusted data, not trusted instructions.

topics.label: Retrieval poisoning
topics.detail: Understand retrieval poisoning and malicious instructions hidden inside indexed documents.

topics.label: Document-level permissions
topics.detail: Enforce document-level permissions so users retrieve only information they are authorized to access.

topics.label: Preventing cross-tenant leakage
topics.detail: Prevent cross-user or cross-tenant data leakage from vector stores and memory systems.

topics.label: Preserving provenance
topics.detail: Preserve source/provenance information for retrieved content.

modules.outcome: Secure the knowledge layer underneath a RAG application.

modules.title: Data privacy, PII & secrets

topics.label: Redaction & minimization

topics.label: Keeping PII out of logs & traces

topics.label: Retention, deletion & residency

topics.label: Private connectivity & zero retention
topics.detail: Use the controls that make regulated deployments possible: private connectivity to the model endpoint, no public egress, and contractual zero-retention or no-training terms.

topics.label: Protecting secrets from the model
topics.detail: Protect secrets so they are never unnecessarily exposed to the model.

modules.outcome: Minimize the amount of sensitive information exposed throughout an AI system.

topics.detail: Build adversarial tests for prompt injection, jailbreaks, malicious documents, tool misuse, data extraction, and unsafe agent actions.

topics.detail: Test RAG systems by injecting malicious content into retrievable documents.

topics.label: Attacking agents through their tools
topics.detail: Test agents by attempting to make them exceed permissions, misuse tools, reveal secrets, or enter loops.

topics.label: Vulnerabilities become regression tests
topics.detail: Turn discovered vulnerabilities into permanent security regression tests.

topics.label: Attack-success & leakage rates
topics.detail: Track measures such as attack-success rate, sensitive-data leakage, and unsafe-action rate where useful.

modules.outcome: Test defenses adversarially instead of assuming they work.
