levels.title: LLMOps: From Development to Production
levels.scope: Take the RAG application and the agent you have already built into production — versioned, evaluated on every change, guarded, containerized, deployed on AWS, and monitored — and keep them improving once real users arrive.

modules.title: What LLMOps adds

topics.label: LLMOps vs MLOps
topics.detail: Understand LLMOps as the practice of shipping, operating, and improving LLM applications, and where it overlaps with and departs from classic MLOps.

topics.label: Application vs model LLMOps
topics.detail: Distinguish application LLMOps, which runs products on top of existing models, from model LLMOps, which trains and hosts the models themselves, and recognize that most teams practise the first.

topics.label: Why LLM systems are hard to operate
topics.detail: Understand what makes LLM systems harder to operate: non-deterministic outputs, prompts that change behavior without a code change, provider-side model updates, and a cost attached to every request.

topics.label: What a release consists of
topics.detail: Define what a release actually is for an LLM application: code, prompts, model version, retrieval configuration, index contents, and tool definitions, all of which must be versioned together.

topics.label: Operating RAG vs agents
topics.detail: Understand how operating a RAG application differs from operating an agent, from stale indexes and retrieval drift on one side to runaway loops and tool failures on the other.

topics.label: The lifecycle of this level
topics.detail: Map the lifecycle this level follows: track → evaluate → guard → serve → ship → deploy → monitor → improve.

modules.outcome: Explain what has to be versioned, tested, and watched for an LLM application to be safe to change.

modules.title: Preparing your apps for production

topics.label: Reuse your Level 4 and 5 apps
topics.detail: Take the RAG application from Level 4 and the agent from Level 5 as the two systems this level operates, rather than building new ones.

topics.label: Configuration, not code
topics.detail: Separate configuration from code, so the model, prompts, retrieval parameters, and tool set can change without a rewrite.

topics.label: Pinned model & dependency versions
topics.detail: Pin model versions and dependency versions, so a rebuild next month produces the same system as today.

topics.label: Traceable from the first request
topics.detail: Make each request traceable from the start by attaching a request ID, the prompt version, and the model version to everything it touches.

topics.label: The Level 7 eval set as yardstick
topics.detail: Carry the evaluation dataset from Level 7 forward as the fixed yardstick every later change will be measured against.

modules.outcome: Have two applications structured so that every behavior-changing setting is explicit, versioned, and recorded.

modules.title: Experiment tracking & prompt versioning

topics.label: Experiments in MLflow
topics.detail: Record each experiment in MLflow with its parameters, such as chunk size, top-k, model, temperature, and tool set.

topics.label: Scores, prompts & outputs per run
topics.detail: Log evaluation scores as metrics and keep prompts, configurations, and sample outputs as artifacts of the run.

topics.label: Comparing runs
topics.detail: Compare runs side by side to see which change actually moved quality, latency, or cost.

topics.label: A baseline before changes
topics.detail: Record a baseline run for both applications before changing anything.

topics.label: A prompt registry
topics.detail: Store prompts in a prompt registry such as Langfuse, so they are versioned, reviewed, and deployed independently of code.

topics.label: Staging & production labels
topics.detail: Label prompt versions for staging and production, and promote a version by moving the label rather than editing text in place.

topics.label: Runtime fetch with a fallback
topics.detail: Fetch prompts at runtime with caching and a pinned fallback, so a registry outage does not take the application down.

topics.label: Rollback by moving a label
topics.detail: Roll back a bad prompt by moving the production label back to the previous version.

topics.label: Traces linked to prompt versions
topics.detail: Link every trace to the prompt version that produced it, so a regression can be traced to the change that caused it.

modules.outcome: Keep a reproducible history of every prompt and configuration, and change either one without a code deployment.

modules.title: Evaluation as a release gate

topics.label: The eval suite as DeepEval tests
topics.detail: Turn the Level 7 evaluation suite into automated tests that run with DeepEval inside an ordinary test runner.

topics.label: RAG & agent metrics
topics.detail: Score the RAG application on faithfulness, answer relevance, and contextual precision, and the agent on tool selection, task completion, and step efficiency.

topics.label: Per-metric thresholds
topics.detail: Set a threshold per metric against the recorded baseline, and fail the build when a change falls below it.

topics.label: Reviewed synthetic cases
topics.detail: Extend coverage with synthetic test cases generated by DeepEval, reviewed by a person before they join the suite.

topics.label: Handling non-determinism
topics.detail: Handle non-determinism by repeating runs, using tolerance bands, and fixing sampling settings where the task allows it.

topics.label: Fast subset vs full suite
topics.detail: Budget evaluation cost and time by running a fast subset on every change and the full suite before release.

topics.label: Prompt & model changes gated too
topics.detail: Treat a prompt change, a model change, and a retrieval change exactly like a code change, so all of them pass through the same gate.

topics.label: Gated runs logged in MLflow
topics.detail: Record every gated run in MLflow, so the history of a metric shows which release moved it.

modules.outcome: Make it impossible for a change that lowers measured quality to reach production unnoticed.

modules.title: Runtime guardrails

topics.label: Level 8 threats as runtime checks
topics.detail: Turn the threat model from Level 8 into runtime checks that run on every request, in front of and behind the model.

topics.label: Schema validation & re-asking
topics.detail: Enforce structured outputs with Guardrails AI, validating against a schema and re-asking the model when validation fails.

topics.label: Topical rails with NeMo Guardrails
topics.detail: Define topical and conversational rails with NeMo Guardrails, and understand when that framework suits better than a validator.

topics.label: Input & output checks
topics.detail: Check inputs for prompt injection attempts and personal data, and outputs for ungrounded claims, off-topic answers, and leaked secrets.

topics.label: Agent tool, step & spend limits
topics.detail: Validate tool arguments before execution, and cap agent steps, retries, and spend per request so a loop cannot run unbounded.

topics.label: Guardrail latency & false positives
topics.detail: Measure what each guardrail costs in latency and how often it blocks a legitimate request.

topics.label: Logging every block
topics.detail: Log every block and every re-ask, so guardrail behavior can be reviewed and tuned rather than trusted blindly.

modules.outcome: Run both applications behind input, output, and agent guardrails whose cost and false-positive rate you have measured.

modules.title: Application serving & containerization

topics.label: A FastAPI backend
topics.detail: Move application logic out of notebooks and scripts into a FastAPI backend with validated requests and typed responses.

topics.label: Streaming with server-sent events
topics.detail: Stream responses token by token with server-sent events, so users see the answer forming instead of waiting for all of it.

topics.label: Timeouts & disconnects
topics.detail: Set timeouts and handle client disconnects, so an abandoned request stops consuming model tokens.

topics.label: Health & readiness endpoints
topics.detail: Expose health and readiness endpoints that report whether the model provider and vector database are reachable.

topics.label: A thin Streamlit frontend
topics.detail: Build a Streamlit frontend that only renders the interface and calls the backend, holding no application logic of its own.

topics.label: Showing streams & errors
topics.detail: Render the streamed response and surface errors, timeouts, and guardrail blocks to the user in plain language.

topics.label: Docker images
topics.detail: Package the backend and frontend as Docker images with small, reproducible builds.

topics.label: The stack in Docker Compose
topics.detail: Run the backend, frontend, and the vector database your RAG application already uses together with Docker Compose.

topics.label: Secrets at runtime, not in images
topics.detail: Supply secrets and API keys through the environment at runtime, never baked into an image.

modules.outcome: Serve both applications as a streaming, containerized stack that runs the same way on any machine.

modules.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

topics.label: Tests → eval gate → build
topics.detail: Build a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs unit tests, then the evaluation gate, then builds an image, in that order.

topics.label: Commit-tagged images
topics.detail: Tag every image with the commit it was built from, and push only images that passed the gate to a registry such as Docker Hub.

topics.label: Pipeline secrets
topics.detail: Store provider keys and registry credentials as pipeline secrets, and keep them out of logs and pull-request builds from forks.

topics.label: Manual approval for production
topics.detail: Require a manual approval before a release reaches production, while allowing staging to deploy automatically.

topics.label: Rollback to a known tag
topics.detail: Keep the previous image deployable, so a rollback is a redeploy of a known tag rather than a rebuild.

modules.outcome: Automate the path from a commit to a tested, tagged, deployable image, with quality enforced before anything ships.

modules.title: Deployment on AWS

topics.label: EC2 with an IAM role
topics.detail: Provision EC2 instances for the application, install Docker, and attach an IAM role instead of storing access keys on the machine.

topics.label: Secrets Manager
topics.detail: Store provider API keys in AWS Secrets Manager and load them when the container starts.

topics.label: Releases with CodeDeploy
topics.detail: Use AWS CodeDeploy to pull a tagged image and replace running containers, with health checks deciding whether the release continues.

topics.label: In-place vs blue/green
topics.detail: Choose between in-place and blue/green releases, and roll back automatically when the new version fails its health checks.

topics.label: Load balancer & streaming timeouts
topics.detail: Put an Application Load Balancer in front of the instances, and raise its idle timeout so long streamed responses are not cut off.

topics.label: Auto Scaling groups
topics.detail: Add an Auto Scaling group that adds instances when busy and removes them when quiet.

topics.label: Scale on concurrency, not CPU
topics.detail: Scale on request concurrency rather than CPU, since an LLM application spends most of its time waiting on the model provider.

topics.label: Provider rate limits cap first
topics.detail: Recognize that provider rate limits usually cap throughput before your servers do, and size scaling with those limits in view.

modules.outcome: Run both applications on AWS with automated releases, health-checked rollbacks, load balancing, and scaling.

modules.title: Monitoring & observability

topics.label: Prometheus & Node Exporter
topics.detail: Run Prometheus to collect metrics from every instance, using Node Exporter for CPU, memory, disk, and network.

topics.label: Application metrics
topics.detail: Export application metrics from the backend: requests, latency percentiles, errors, model calls, tokens, and guardrail blocks.

topics.label: Grafana dashboards
topics.detail: Build Grafana dashboards that show server health, traffic, latency, error rate, and token spend side by side.

topics.label: Alerts that need a human
topics.detail: Alert on the signals that need a human, such as error-rate spikes, latency beyond budget, failed scaling, and spend above a daily limit.

topics.label: Tracing in Langfuse
topics.detail: Trace every request in Langfuse through retrieval, model calls, and tool calls, with latency and cost recorded at each step.

topics.label: Online evals & user feedback
topics.detail: Run online evaluations on a sample of live traffic, and collect user feedback alongside them.

topics.label: Failures back into the suite
topics.detail: Turn production failures found in traces and feedback into new cases for the Level 7 evaluation suite.

modules.outcome: See server health, application behavior, cost, and answer quality for the live system, and feed what you find back into evaluation.

modules.title: Incidents, rollbacks & change management

topics.label: LLM-specific incidents
topics.detail: Recognize the incidents specific to LLM applications: a provider outage, a silent model update, a prompt regression, a stale index, a runaway agent, and a cost spike.

topics.label: The lever for each cause
topics.detail: Respond with the lever that matches the cause: a model fallback, a prompt rollback, an image rollback, an index rebuild, or a spend cap.

topics.label: Runbooks
topics.detail: Write a short runbook per incident type, naming the signal that detects it, the first action to take, and the person who decides.

topics.label: Re-evaluate on model changes
topics.detail: Re-run the evaluation suite whenever the provider announces a model change, before the change reaches your users.

topics.label: Blameless reviews
topics.detail: Run a blameless review after each incident, and add the case that caused it to the evaluation suite.

modules.outcome: Detect, contain, and recover from LLM-specific incidents with a practised response rather than improvisation.

projects.title: Capstone: LLMOps Project
projects.result: a deployed LLM application where every change is versioned and evaluated before release, and whose health, quality, and cost you can see while it runs.

checklist.label: One app, the whole lifecycle
checklist.detail: Take the agent from Level 5 or the RAG application from Level 4 through the whole lifecycle of this level.

checklist.label: Versioned prompts & tracked runs
checklist.detail: Version every prompt in a registry with a production label, and record experiments with their parameters, metrics, and artifacts.

checklist.label: A CI gate that blocks a regression
checklist.detail: Gate every change in CI with the evaluation suite, and show the gate blocking a deliberately regressed prompt.

checklist.label: Guardrails with logged blocks
checklist.detail: Run the application behind input, output, and agent guardrails, with every block logged.

checklist.label: A streaming stack in Compose
checklist.detail: Serve it as a streaming FastAPI backend and a Streamlit frontend, packaged with Docker Compose.

checklist.label: CI/CD to EC2 via CodeDeploy
checklist.detail: Build and push commit-tagged images through GitHub Actions, and deploy them to EC2 with CodeDeploy behind a load balancer with Auto Scaling and Secrets Manager.

checklist.label: Dashboards, alerts & traces
checklist.detail: Monitor it with Grafana dashboards and at least one working alert, and trace requests with cost and latency per step.

checklist.label: A rollback & a runbook
checklist.detail: Demonstrate one rollback, of either a prompt or an image, and write the runbook for one incident type.

levels.title: Managed AI Platforms
levels.scope: Ship an AI application on the platforms teams actually buy — a cloud provider's managed platform, an open-weight hosting provider, or a router spanning several — and know which parts to hand over and which to keep.

modules.title: The three ways to consume a model

topics.label: Three ways to consume a model
topics.detail: Understand the three paths an organization can take: a provider's public API, a managed platform inside its own cloud account, or open weights it hosts itself or through an inference provider.

topics.label: Open weights without running GPUs
topics.detail: Recognize that open weights no longer imply operating GPUs, since managed platforms and inference providers serve the same open models on demand.

topics.label: Why regulated teams cannot use a public API
topics.detail: Understand why most regulated organizations cannot use a public API directly, and why that constraint decides architecture long before quality does.

topics.label: Comparing the three paths
topics.detail: Compare the three paths on identity, data handling, region, capacity, price per token, operational effort, and how quickly new models reach you.

topics.label: Platform, gateway, or both
topics.detail: Understand where a managed platform sits relative to the model gateway pattern: it can be your gateway, sit behind one, or be one provider among several that a gateway routes to.

modules.outcome: Place any AI workload on the right consumption path and defend the choice with reasons other than familiarity.

modules.title: Platform anatomy: Bedrock, Vertex AI & Azure AI Foundry

topics.label: The shape all three share
topics.detail: Understand the shape all three share: a catalog of closed and open-weight models, one endpoint style, one identity system, one network boundary, and one bill.

topics.label: Reading a model catalog
topics.detail: Read a platform's model catalog the way you read a model card, noting which providers are offered, which regions carry them, and which versions are pinned or retired.

topics.label: Invoking through the platform
topics.detail: Understand how invocation differs from a provider SDK, including the platform's own request format, its converse-style unified API, and the provider-native passthrough where one exists.

topics.label: Same ideas, different vocabulary
topics.detail: Recognize the platform-specific vocabulary for the same ideas, so a Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Azure AI Foundry document reads as a variation rather than a new subject.

topics.label: Calling a hosted model
topics.detail: Call a hosted model on one platform from application code and confirm the response, usage, and cost reporting you get back.

topics.label: Swapping models inside one catalog
topics.detail: Compare the same prompt across two models in the same catalog without changing how you authenticate, network, or bill.

topics.label: What the platform does not give you
topics.detail: Understand what the platform does not give you: prompt quality, retrieval design, evaluation depth, and product behavior remain yours.

modules.outcome: Work confidently on at least one managed platform and map its concepts onto the other two.

modules.title: Identity, networking & tenancy

topics.label: Cloud identity instead of API keys
topics.detail: Replace API keys with cloud identity: roles, service accounts, and workload identity that grant a service the right to invoke a model.

topics.label: Least privilege for model access
topics.detail: Apply least privilege to model access, scoping which models, regions, and actions an application or team may use.

topics.label: Auditing who invoked what
topics.detail: Understand how platform access is audited, and why an audit trail of who invoked which model matters in regulated environments.

topics.label: Private connectivity, no public egress
topics.detail: Reach a model over private connectivity so requests never traverse the public internet, and understand what that buys you and what it costs.

topics.label: Tenant isolation on shared infrastructure
topics.detail: Design tenant isolation on a shared platform: separate accounts or projects, scoped credentials, per-tenant keys, and retrieval that cannot cross a tenant boundary.

topics.label: Encryption & customer-managed keys
topics.detail: Understand encryption and key management options, including customer-managed keys for data at rest.

modules.outcome: Deploy an AI workload whose identity, network path, and tenant boundaries would survive a security review.

modules.title: Regions, residency & compliance

topics.label: Models exist per region
topics.detail: Understand that a model exists in specific regions, and that the region you are permitted to use often decides which models you may design around.

topics.label: Data residency & localization
topics.detail: Plan for data residency requirements, including Indian data-localization expectations and the sector rules that sit above them.

topics.label: Retention & training terms in writing
topics.detail: Understand retention and training terms in writing: what the platform logs, for how long, who can see it, and whether your data may be used to improve a model.

topics.label: Connecting back to governance
topics.detail: Connect these controls to the governance work of Level 8, where residency, deletion, and third-party processing were named as requirements.

topics.label: When your model is not in your region
topics.detail: Handle the common case where the model you want is unavailable in your required region, through cross-region reasoning, a different model, or an exception you can document.

modules.outcome: State, for a given workload, exactly where the data goes, where it is processed, how long it is kept, and under whose terms.

modules.title: Capacity, quotas & cost

topics.label: On-demand vs provisioned throughput
topics.detail: Distinguish on-demand capacity from provisioned or reserved throughput, and understand why committed capacity changes both price and rate limits.

topics.label: Reading the quota model
topics.detail: Read the quota model of a platform: requests per minute, tokens per minute, concurrent requests, and per-model limits that differ by region.

topics.label: Planning for burst traffic
topics.detail: Plan for burst traffic with queueing, backpressure, and batch endpoints instead of assuming the platform will absorb a spike.

topics.label: Defending a quota increase
topics.detail: Request and defend a quota increase with traffic evidence, since capacity is an approval process rather than a setting.

topics.label: Cost per request, end to end
topics.detail: Model cost per request end to end, including input and output tokens, retrieval calls, and any managed component you invoke along the way.

topics.label: Attributing spend per team or tenant
topics.detail: Attribute cost to a project, team, or tenant using the platform's own tagging and billing views, which a shared API key cannot do.

topics.label: Budgets & runaway-cost alerts
topics.detail: Set budgets and alerts so a runaway agent loop is caught by spend monitoring rather than by the monthly invoice.

topics.label: Which pricing model wins at your volume
topics.detail: Compare on-demand, committed, and self-hosted economics at your actual volume rather than at the volume in the pricing example.

modules.outcome: Size capacity and forecast spend for a real workload, and know at what volume each pricing model wins.

modules.title: Open-weight model platforms

topics.label: The open-weight hosting ladder
topics.detail: Understand the spectrum between calling an API and operating hardware: model hubs, serverless inference providers, GPU compute platforms, and your own servers.

topics.label: Model hubs & checkpoint trust
topics.detail: Use a model hub such as Hugging Face to find open-weight models, read their cards, check licences and gated access, and judge whether a checkpoint is trustworthy.

topics.label: Serverless inference providers
topics.detail: Call an open-weight model through a serverless inference provider such as Together, Fireworks, Groq, or Replicate, where you pay per token and never see a GPU.

topics.label: GPU compute platforms
topics.detail: Understand what a GPU compute platform such as Modal, Baseten, or RunPod adds: you bring the serving stack and they schedule, scale, and bill the hardware.

topics.label: Serving it yourself with vLLM
topics.detail: Serve a model yourself with vLLM, TGI, or Ollama, and understand continuous batching, KV-cache reuse, and why a naive request loop wastes most of a GPU.

topics.label: Per-token vs per-GPU-hour
topics.detail: Compare per-token pricing with per-GPU-hour pricing, and find the utilization point at which renting hardware becomes cheaper than paying per token.

topics.label: Cold starts & scale-to-zero
topics.detail: Understand cold starts and scale-to-zero, and why a deployment that idles cheaply may answer its first request slowly.

topics.label: Sizing hardware for a model
topics.detail: Size hardware for a model from parameter count, precision, quantization, and KV-cache growth with context length, since memory decides which GPU you need.

topics.label: What hosting open weights buys
topics.detail: Understand what hosting open weights gives you — predictable cost at volume, data that never leaves your boundary, and full control of versions — and what it asks of you in return.

topics.label: Open vs closed on your own task
topics.detail: Evaluate an open-weight model against a closed one on your own task before assuming that either is obviously better.

modules.outcome: Run an open-weight model on the right rung of the hosting ladder and justify the choice on cost, latency, control, and effort.

modules.title: Model routers & LLM gateways

topics.label: One endpoint, many providers
topics.detail: Understand a gateway as one endpoint in front of many providers: it holds the credentials, accepts one request format, and hides which model actually served the request.

topics.label: Hosted routers vs self-hosted proxies
topics.detail: Compare hosted routers such as OpenRouter and Portkey with self-hosted proxies such as LiteLLM, and with the routing built into cloud platforms and framework gateways.

topics.label: Routing rules & automatic failover
topics.detail: Route by rule — task type, cost ceiling, context length, latency target, region, or risk — and fail over automatically when a provider errors or throttles.

topics.label: Virtual keys, budgets & quotas
topics.detail: Use a gateway's spend controls: virtual keys per team or per feature, budgets, quotas, and per-key rate limits that stop one client exhausting shared capacity.

topics.label: One view of usage and cost
topics.detail: Get one view of usage, latency, errors, and cost across every provider instead of stitching separate dashboards together.

topics.label: The router is on the critical path
topics.detail: Understand the failure mode you have introduced, since a gateway now sits on the critical path and needs its own availability, timeouts, and a bypass plan.

topics.label: Differences a router cannot hide
topics.detail: Handle the provider differences a gateway cannot hide: tool-calling formats, structured-output support, token limits, and prompts that behave differently on each model.

topics.label: Caching at the gateway
topics.detail: Cache at the gateway, both exact-match and semantic, and decide which requests must never be answered from a cache.

topics.label: When a router earns its place
topics.detail: Decide when a router earns its place — several providers, several teams, or spend worth governing — and when one provider and a client library is the honest answer.

topics.label: Routing changes who answers
topics.detail: Keep evals in the loop, because a routing rule change swaps the model answering your users without a single line of application code changing.

modules.outcome: Run model traffic through a router that gives you failover, spend control, and one view of usage, without pretending that providers are interchangeable.

modules.title: Managed building blocks: build or buy

topics.label: Managed retrieval & knowledge bases
topics.detail: Understand managed retrieval offerings such as knowledge bases and enterprise search, which package ingestion, chunking, embedding, and retrieval behind a configuration.

topics.label: Managed retrieval vs your own stack
topics.detail: Compare a managed knowledge base with the retrieval stack you built in Level 4 on control over chunking, retrieval tuning, evaluation depth, and cost at your corpus size.

topics.label: Managed agent & workflow runtimes
topics.detail: Understand managed agent and workflow runtimes, and what they assume about tools, memory, and orchestration compared with the agents you built in Level 5.

topics.label: Managed guardrails
topics.detail: Understand managed guardrails for content filtering, topic restriction, and sensitive-data redaction, and where they sit relative to your own checks.

topics.label: Managed evaluation
topics.detail: Understand managed evaluation offerings and judge whether their metrics answer the questions your eval suite from Level 7 was built to answer.

topics.label: Managed fine-tuning & distillation
topics.detail: Understand managed fine-tuning and distillation, including which base models can be adapted, where the resulting weights live, and whether you can take them with you.

topics.label: Deciding layer by layer
topics.detail: Decide each layer separately, since adopting a managed retrieval service does not commit you to managed agents, guardrails, or evaluation.

topics.label: What to judge each candidate on
topics.detail: Judge each candidate on control, transparency, evaluation depth, cost at your volume, and how much of the behavior you must be able to explain to an auditor.

topics.label: Measuring the portability cost
topics.detail: Measure the portability cost before adopting: a prompt moves between providers in minutes, while a knowledge base, agent, or guardrail configuration usually does not.

topics.label: When buying is the honest call
topics.detail: Recognize the honest cases for buying: a small team, a standard use case, a compliance deadline, or a workload whose quality bar the managed component already clears.

modules.outcome: Make a defensible build-or-buy call for every layer of an AI system instead of adopting or rejecting managed services wholesale.

modules.title: Portability, lock-in & migration

topics.label: What travels and what does not
topics.detail: Separate what is portable from what is not: prompts, evals, and application code travel easily, while managed indexes, agent definitions, and platform-specific APIs do not.

topics.label: Keeping an abstraction in place
topics.detail: Keep an abstraction between application code and provider so a model swap is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

topics.label: The real costs of lock-in
topics.detail: Understand the real costs of lock-in beyond price: model availability, feature pace, negotiating position, and the work of proving a new platform is safe.

topics.label: Migration as an evaluation exercise
topics.detail: Plan a migration between platforms or providers as an evaluation exercise, re-running your eval suite before, during, and after the move.

topics.label: Catalog lag & deprecation
topics.detail: Handle catalog lag and platform-side deprecation, since managed catalogs trail the frontier and retire versions on their own schedule.

topics.label: Running two platforms in parallel
topics.detail: Run two platforms in parallel where the workload justifies it, using a gateway to route by capability, region, cost, or availability.

topics.label: Multi-cloud, honestly
topics.detail: Understand multi-cloud honestly: it buys resilience and leverage, and it costs duplicated evaluation, duplicated security review, and duplicated operational knowledge.

modules.outcome: Adopt a platform without being trapped by it, and move a workload between platforms without discovering the coupling too late.

modules.title: Capstone: deploy on a managed platform

projects.title: Capstone: deploy on a managed platform
projects.result: the same application, running where a regulated employer could actually run it, with the identity, network, residency, capacity, cost, and portability decisions written down.

checklist.label: Redeploy an app you already built
checklist.detail: Take an application you built in an earlier level and redeploy it against a managed platform, keeping the behavior and changing the plumbing.

checklist.label: Cloud identity, no API key
checklist.detail: Authenticate through cloud identity with least-privilege access to a named set of models, and remove the provider API key from the application entirely.

checklist.label: Private path & recorded data handling
checklist.detail: Route model traffic over a private network path, and record where the data is processed, how long it is retained, and under which terms.

checklist.label: One component bought, one built
checklist.detail: Replace at least one hand-built component with a managed equivalent, and keep at least one hand-built because you can defend why.

checklist.label: Re-run your evals after the move
checklist.detail: Re-run your evaluation suite on the migrated system and report what changed in quality, latency, and cost.

checklist.label: A gateway with a working fallback
checklist.detail: Route the application's model calls through a gateway with a working fallback, or state why direct calls to one provider are enough at your scale.

checklist.label: Capacity sizing & budget alert
checklist.detail: Size capacity for your expected traffic, set a budget alert, and state the volume at which a different pricing model would win.

checklist.label: A platform decision record
checklist.detail: Write a one-page platform decision record: the workload, the constraints, the path chosen, the components bought and built, and the exit plan.

levels.title: Multimodal 101: Beyond Text
levels.scope: Build a strong mental model of how models handle images, audio, and video, why they fail differently from text models, and how to choose and use the right model when a task stops being text-only.

modules.title: Beyond text: what a multimodal model is

topics.label: What makes a model multimodal
topics.detail: Understand what makes a model multimodal: images, audio, and video are converted into tokens and fed into the same transformer that already processes text.

topics.label: Native multimodal vs bolted-on pipeline
topics.detail: Distinguish a natively multimodal model, trained on mixed data from the start, from a pipeline that bolts a separate transcription, OCR, or captioning model in front of a text-only LLM.

topics.label: Text as the interlingua
topics.detail: Understand why text remains the interlingua: whatever enters the model, the reasoning and almost always the output happen in tokens that behave like text.

topics.label: What carries over from text LLMs
topics.detail: Build intuition for what changes and what does not: the context window, tokenization, sampling, and failure modes you learned for text all still apply.

topics.label: What "any-to-any" really means
topics.detail: Recognize what "any-to-any" marketing does and does not mean today, since most models accept several input modalities but produce only text.

topics.label: What a pipeline throws away
topics.detail: Understand why a bolted-on pipeline loses information that a native model keeps, such as tone in speech or layout in a scanned page.

modules.outcome: Explain to someone what a multimodal model actually is, and tell whether a given product is using a native model or a pipeline stitched together around a text model.

modules.title: Vision: how images become tokens

topics.label: Patches & the vision encoder
topics.detail: Understand how a vision encoder splits an image into a grid of patches and turns each patch into a vector the transformer can consume.

topics.label: Why one image costs many tokens
topics.detail: Build intuition for why a single image can cost hundreds or thousands of tokens, and why that cost scales with resolution rather than with file size.

topics.label: Tiling & detail settings
topics.detail: Understand tiling and detail settings: high-detail modes slice a large image into multiple tiles, each priced as its own set of tokens.

topics.label: What downscaling destroys
topics.detail: Recognize what downscaling and aspect-ratio changes destroy, especially small text, thin lines, dense tables, and fine chart labels.

topics.label: Images share the context window
topics.detail: Understand that image tokens occupy the same context window as text tokens, so a handful of screenshots can crowd out the instructions and history around them.

topics.label: Full image, crops, or overview
topics.detail: Understand the practical trade-off between sending one large detailed image, several cropped regions, or a downscaled overview.

modules.outcome: Predict roughly what an image will cost in tokens and choose a resolution and cropping strategy instead of uploading whatever the camera produced.

modules.title: Vision: capabilities & failure modes

topics.label: What vision models do well
topics.detail: Understand what vision models genuinely do well: reading text in images, describing scenes, extracting named fields from documents, and interpreting charts at a coarse level.

topics.label: Counting, space & dense tables
topics.detail: Understand the failure modes that repeat across models: precise counting, spatial and geometric reasoning, dense small text, and exact row-to-column alignment in tables.

topics.label: Fabricated visual detail
topics.detail: Recognize fabricated detail, where a model confidently reports values, labels, or objects that a low-resolution or ambiguous image never actually contained.

topics.label: Why vision failures happen
topics.detail: Understand why these failures happen: the model is generating a plausible description of an image it perceives as patches, not measuring or verifying anything.

topics.label: Asking "how reliably?" for images
topics.detail: Adopt the engineering question for vision too: not "can this model read invoices?", but "how reliably does it read my invoices, at my resolution, in my formats?".

topics.label: Safeguards when reliability is short
topics.detail: Understand which safeguards apply when reliability is not enough, such as higher resolution, cropping, structured output, verification passes, or human review.

modules.outcome: Predict which visual tasks a model will handle unaided and which need cropping, higher resolution, or a verification step before you can ship them.

modules.title: Vision: documents, charts & visual RAG

topics.label: Text-layer PDFs vs scans
topics.detail: Distinguish a digital PDF that carries its own text layer from a scan or photograph where every character has to be recovered from pixels.

topics.label: OCR vs native vision reading
topics.detail: Compare OCR-based reading with native vision reading by a multimodal model on accuracy, cost, latency, and how much layout they preserve.

topics.label: Layout & reading order
topics.detail: Understand why reading order matters: multi-column pages, headers, footers, footnotes, and sidebars can turn a correct page into nonsense when flattened badly.

topics.label: Tables, forms & merged cells
topics.detail: Read tables and forms reliably, including merged cells, multi-page tables, checkboxes, and key-value layouts where the label and the value sit far apart.

topics.label: How models read charts
topics.detail: Understand what a model actually does with a chart: it reads axes, labels, and legends rather than the underlying numbers, so precise values are often estimated.

topics.label: Schema before prompt
topics.detail: Define the schema before the prompt: name the fields you need, their types, and which of them are required, instead of asking for a free-form summary.

topics.label: Extract & validate fields
topics.detail: Extract fields from a document with a vision model and validate the result against that schema, checking types, ranges, dates, totals, and required values.

topics.label: Grounding fields to page regions
topics.detail: Ground every extracted field in its source by returning the page number or region it came from, so a human can verify a value without rereading the document.

topics.label: Document failure modes
topics.detail: Recognize document-specific failure modes: invented values in blank cells, rows merged across page breaks, confused units or currencies, and misread handwriting.

topics.label: Routing low confidence to review
topics.detail: Route low-confidence extractions to human review rather than letting an uncertain value flow silently into a database.

topics.label: Pages & regions as retrieval units
topics.detail: Understand what changes when the retrieval unit is a page image or a region of a page rather than a chunk of text, and how embeddings are produced for it.

topics.label: Hybrid text + visual retrieval
topics.detail: Build hybrid retrieval that searches extracted text and page images together, and recognize which of the two wins for a given question.

topics.label: Citing the page you answered from
topics.detail: Cite the page or region an answer came from, so the reader can open the document at the right place and check it.

topics.label: When plain text beats visual
topics.detail: Compare a visual pipeline with a plain text pipeline on cost, latency, and accuracy, and understand why clean digital text rarely needs page images at all.

topics.label: The token cost of page images
topics.detail: Understand the practical cost of visual RAG: page images consume far more tokens than the equivalent text, which changes both latency and price per query.

modules.outcome: Build a document pipeline that reads real-world PDFs and scans, extracts validated fields, and answers questions with a citation back to the page it used.

modules.title: Vision: image & video generation

topics.label: Denoising, not next-token prediction
topics.detail: Understand that a generative image model starts from random noise and repeatedly removes it, rather than predicting the next token the way an LLM does.

topics.label: What a prompt controls
topics.detail: Understand what a prompt actually controls in image generation: subject, composition, style, and detail, with far less literal instruction-following than a text model offers.

topics.label: Seeds & reproducibility
topics.detail: Understand seeds and reproducibility: the same prompt with the same seed returns the same image, while a new seed produces a different interpretation of the same words.

topics.label: Resolution, steps & cost
topics.detail: Understand how resolution, aspect ratio, and step count affect quality, generation time, and cost.

topics.label: img2img, inpainting & outpainting
topics.detail: Distinguish text-to-image from image-to-image, inpainting, and outpainting, and recognize which one a given editing task actually needs.

topics.label: Style & structural control
topics.detail: Understand reference and style conditioning, along with structural control such as pose, depth, or edge guidance, for when a prompt alone cannot hold a layout steady.

topics.label: Cost per accepted image
topics.detail: Build intuition for iteration cost: generation is cheap per image but expensive per accepted image, because most candidates are discarded.

topics.label: What video adds: time & motion
topics.detail: Understand what video generation adds: time, motion, and consistency across frames, which makes length, cost, and failure modes grow quickly.

topics.label: Provenance, watermarks & rights
topics.detail: Understand provenance and rights: watermarking, content credentials, training-data licensing, and the commercial-use terms attached to generated assets.

modules.outcome: Produce and iteratively control generated images, and judge whether a generation task is worth its cost in review time and rights risk.

modules.title: Audio: how sound becomes tokens

topics.label: Waveform to spectrogram to tokens
topics.detail: Understand the path from a waveform to model input: audio is sampled, converted into a spectrogram or learned audio tokens, and then treated as another token stream.

topics.label: Cost per second, not per word
topics.detail: Build intuition for audio cost and latency, where tokens accumulate per second of duration rather than per word, so silence and background noise are paid for too.

topics.label: Transcribe-then-prompt vs audio-native
topics.detail: Distinguish transcribe-then-prompt pipelines, where a speech-to-text model produces text for an LLM, from audio-native models that consume the sound itself.

topics.label: What a transcript discards
topics.detail: Understand what a transcript discards: tone, emphasis, hesitation, overlapping speakers, emotion, and everything that separates "fine" said warmly from "fine" said flatly.

topics.label: Why audio is latency-sensitive
topics.detail: Recognize why audio input and output are latency-sensitive, since a conversation is judged on response delay in a way that a document summary never is.

topics.label: Where speech recognition breaks
topics.detail: Understand common audio failure modes such as accented speech, code-switching between languages, domain jargon, poor microphones, and long silences.

modules.outcome: Choose between a transcription pipeline and an audio-native model for a given task, and explain what each choice costs you in fidelity, latency, and money.

modules.title: Audio: speech to text & text to speech

topics.label: What Whisper actually returns
topics.detail: Understand what a speech-to-text model such as Whisper produces: a transcript, optional word timestamps, and confidence signals rather than clean edited prose.

topics.label: Batch vs streaming transcription
topics.detail: Distinguish batch transcription of a complete recording from streaming transcription, where partial text is emitted while the speaker is still talking.

topics.label: Accents, code-mixing & noise
topics.detail: Understand what degrades transcription in practice — accents, code-mixed Hindi-English speech, background noise, and poor microphones — and supply domain vocabulary as hints.

topics.label: Speaker diarization
topics.detail: Use speaker diarization to attribute each segment to a speaker, and understand why it is a separate step that fails in its own ways.

topics.label: Word error rate in practice
topics.detail: Read word error rate as a measure of transcription quality, and reason about which errors actually matter for whatever happens downstream.

topics.label: What Kokoro turns text into
topics.detail: Understand what a text-to-speech model such as Kokoro turns text into: sampled audio in a chosen voice, produced in one pass or streamed as it is generated.

topics.label: Voice choice & prosody
topics.detail: Choose a voice and shape prosody through pace, pauses, and emphasis, and understand how much control a given model actually exposes.

topics.label: Pronunciation control
topics.detail: Control the pronunciation of names, acronyms, numbers, and code-mixed text, since these are where synthetic speech usually embarrasses itself.

topics.label: Streaming synthesis
topics.detail: Stream synthesis so the first audio reaches the listener while the rest is still being generated, instead of waiting for the whole utterance.

topics.label: Hosted vs local speech models
topics.detail: Compare hosted and locally run speech models on cost, latency, privacy, and voice quality, and choose per workload rather than by default.

modules.outcome: Build a speech pipeline that transcribes real recordings and speaks generated text back, with a clear view of where accuracy and latency are lost.

modules.title: Audio: realtime voice agents

topics.label: Latency as the design constraint
topics.detail: Understand why a voice conversation feels broken above roughly a second of silence, and treat end-to-end latency as the primary design constraint.

topics.label: Where the milliseconds go
topics.detail: Break the latency budget into its parts: capture, network, transcription, model thinking, synthesis, and playback.

topics.label: Cascaded vs speech-to-speech
topics.detail: Distinguish a cascaded pipeline, where speech-to-text, an LLM, and text-to-speech run in sequence, from a speech-to-speech realtime API that takes audio in and returns audio.

topics.label: Comparing the two architectures
topics.detail: Compare the two architectures on latency, control, cost, debuggability, and how much of the conversation you can inspect afterwards.

topics.label: What can overlap
topics.detail: Understand which parts can overlap: synthesis can begin before the model has finished, and transcription can run while the user is still speaking.

topics.label: Voice activity detection & endpointing
topics.detail: Understand voice activity detection and endpointing as the mechanism that decides when the user has actually stopped speaking.

topics.label: Why endpointing is hard
topics.detail: Recognize why endpointing is hard: pauses for thought, slow speakers, and background chatter all look like the end of a turn.

topics.label: Barge-in & interruption
topics.detail: Handle barge-in, where the user interrupts mid-answer, by stopping playback and discarding the rest of the planned response.

topics.label: Acting on partial transcripts
topics.detail: Use partial transcripts to start work early, and understand the risk of acting on text the user has not finished saying.

topics.label: State after a cut-short turn
topics.detail: Keep conversation state consistent when a turn is cut short, so the model does not believe it said something the user never heard.

topics.label: Silence, dead air & dropped calls
topics.detail: Handle silence, dead air, and network loss with holding phrases, reconnection, and a graceful exit rather than an unexplained pause.

topics.label: Noise, crosstalk & bad mics
topics.detail: Understand what background noise, crosstalk, and poor microphones do to a live pipeline, and where to place the safeguards.

topics.label: Staying alive during tool calls
topics.detail: Keep the conversation alive while a tool call runs, since a lookup that takes three seconds is silence the user will not tolerate.

topics.label: What to say while waiting
topics.detail: Decide what the agent says while it waits, and what it does when the tool fails or returns nothing useful.

topics.label: Reconstructing a bad call
topics.detail: Capture what a voice session needs for later reconstruction: audio, transcript, timings, and turn boundaries.

modules.outcome: Ship a voice agent that holds a natural conversation: it knows when you stopped talking, it can be interrupted, and it keeps silence short enough to feel human.

modules.title: Cross-modal search & retrieval

topics.label: A shared embedding space
topics.detail: Understand a shared embedding space, where an image and a caption that describe the same thing land close together as vectors.

topics.label: CLIP-style joint embeddings
topics.detail: Understand CLIP-style joint embeddings, where two encoders are trained so that matching image-text pairs are pulled together and mismatched pairs pushed apart.

topics.label: Searching across modalities
topics.detail: Search images with a text query and search text with an image query, using the same vector-search machinery Level 4 introduced for text.

topics.label: Cross-modal vs caption-then-search
topics.detail: Distinguish cross-modal retrieval from captioning every image first and searching the captions, and recognize when each approach wins.

topics.label: Where cross-modal retrieval fails
topics.detail: Recognize where cross-modal retrieval fails: fine-grained detail, text inside images, counting, and domain-specific imagery the encoder never saw.

topics.label: Evaluating on your own collection
topics.detail: Evaluate retrieval quality on your own images and queries rather than trusting a benchmark score measured on a general image collection.

modules.outcome: Decide when a task needs cross-modal retrieval and build a small image-and-text search over your own collection.

modules.title: Choosing a multimodal model

topics.label: Start from the modalities
topics.detail: Start from the modalities themselves: list what must go in, whether text, images, audio, video, or documents, and what must come out.

topics.label: Per-image & per-minute pricing
topics.detail: Understand how multimodal pricing works, since per-image and per-audio-minute charges sit alongside per-token pricing and cost stops being about text length alone.

topics.label: The context cost of images
topics.detail: Understand the context cost of images, where a single image consumes a large, resolution-dependent share of the context window and limits how many you can pass at once.

topics.label: Latency by modality
topics.detail: Compare latency expectations by modality, including time to first audio for streaming voice, where a delay is heard by the user rather than merely measured.

topics.label: API vs self-hosting
topics.detail: Weigh API access against self-hosting for vision and speech, where open models are strong and per-minute costs at volume can outgrow the operational effort.

topics.label: Privacy for voice, faces & scans
topics.detail: Treat privacy as a harder constraint here, because voices, faces, and scanned documents carry consent and data-residency obligations that plain text often does not.

topics.label: Managed speech, vision & document services
topics.detail: Consider managed speech, vision, and document services from the cloud platforms alongside general multimodal models, since a narrow managed service is often cheaper and more accurate at one job.

topics.label: Shortlist, then test your own data
topics.detail: Shortlist two or three candidates, then test them on your own images, recordings, and documents before committing, exactly as you would for a text model.

modules.outcome: Choose a model for a multimodal task on modality support, cost per unit, latency, and privacy, verified against your own examples.

modules.title: Deep research & long-horizon scenarios

topics.label: Why long runs are different
topics.detail: Understand what changes when a task runs for many minutes across many sources instead of resolving inside a single prompt and a single response.

topics.label: Decomposing a research question
topics.detail: Decompose a research question into sub-questions that can be investigated independently, and recognize when a question is too vague to decompose yet.

topics.label: Breadth first, then depth
topics.detail: Search broadly before going deep: gather many candidate sources first, judge which few are worth reading closely, and discard the rest deliberately.

topics.label: Reading sources critically
topics.detail: Read sources critically rather than accumulating them, distinguishing primary evidence, secondary commentary, marketing material, and outdated claims.

topics.label: Reconciling disagreement
topics.detail: Reconcile sources that disagree by preferring better evidence, stating the disagreement explicitly, or reporting genuine uncertainty instead of averaging the answers.

topics.label: Claims attached to sources
topics.detail: Keep every claim attached to the source it came from, so a reader can verify any individual statement without repeating the whole search.

topics.label: Notes and interim summaries
topics.detail: Manage a run that outlives its context by writing notes and interim summaries as the work proceeds, and by carrying forward findings rather than raw source text.

topics.label: Knowing when to stop
topics.detail: Recognize the stopping conditions of a research run: the question is answered, the sources have started repeating, or the remaining uncertainty cannot be resolved by more searching.

topics.label: A report a human can audit
topics.detail: Produce a structured report a human can audit, with the question, the answer, the supporting evidence, the contradictions found, and the gaps that remain.

topics.label: How long runs fail
topics.detail: Understand the characteristic failures of long-horizon runs: drifting away from the original question, confident synthesis of thin evidence, and citations that do not support the sentence attached to them.

modules.outcome: Run a long-horizon research task that produces a cited, structured report whose claims a reader can check individually.

modules.title: On-device & edge modalities

topics.label: Why modalities suit the device
topics.detail: Understand why speech and vision suit on-device execution, since the models are small, the input is private, and the network round trip is often the slowest part.

topics.label: Quantization & what it costs
topics.detail: Understand quantization as trading numerical precision for size and speed, and recognize the tasks where that trade shows up first as degraded quality.

topics.label: Phone & laptop hardware limits
topics.detail: Build intuition for hardware limits on phones and laptops, including memory ceilings, thermal throttling, and battery cost during sustained inference.

topics.label: What on-device buys you
topics.detail: Understand what on-device execution buys you: offline operation, no per-request cost, predictable latency, and data that never leaves the user's machine.

topics.label: On-device, self-hosted or API
topics.detail: Choose deliberately between on-device, self-hosted, and API execution for each modality, since one application can reasonably use all three at once.

modules.outcome: Decide which parts of a multimodal system belong on the user's device and accept the quality trade knowingly.

projects.title: Capstone: ship a multimodal build
projects.result: a working multimodal application that survives real inputs, whose latency and cost you can quote, and whose limitations you can state precisely.

checklist.label: Pick one realistic build
checklist.detail: Choose one realistic build and take it all the way: a voice agent, a document-understanding pipeline, a visual search tool, or a research-report generator.

checklist.label: At least two modalities
checklist.detail: Combine at least two modalities in a single application so the build exercises a real cross-modal boundary rather than one model in isolation.

checklist.label: Real inputs, not samples
checklist.detail: Feed the system real inputs from your own domain, including the messy scans, accented speech, and awkward layouts that curated sample files never contain.

checklist.label: Modality-specific failures
checklist.detail: Handle the modality-specific failures your build will actually hit, such as unreadable regions, silence and background noise, hallucinated chart values, or ambiguous references.

checklist.label: Latency and cost per request
checklist.detail: Measure latency and cost per request, and report them broken down by modality so the expensive part of the pipeline is visible.

checklist.label: Document one real failure
checklist.detail: Document one failure you found by testing on real inputs, explaining what broke, how you detected it, and what you changed in response.

checklist.label: Runnable by someone else
checklist.detail: Package the build so another person can run it from a README with their own inputs, their own credentials, and no help from you.

levels.title: Fine-Tuning
levels.scope: Fine-tune a model only when prompting, retrieval, and orchestration have measurably run out, and prove with evaluation numbers that the tune was worth its data, training, and serving cost.

modules.title: Should you fine-tune?

topics.label: Fine-tuning as the costliest option
topics.detail: Decide between a better prompt, retrieval, tool use, a stronger base model, fine-tuning, or a combination, and treat fine-tuning as the most expensive option on that list.

topics.label: What fine-tuning is good for
topics.detail: Understand what fine-tuning is good for: consistent behavior and style, output formats a prompt cannot hold, narrow structured tasks, shorter prompts, and specializing a smaller model.

topics.label: What it is not good for
topics.detail: Understand what fine-tuning is usually not good for: teaching facts that change, which retrieval can supply fresh, and fixing a task nobody has yet defined well enough to evaluate.

topics.label: Start from a measured failure
topics.detail: Start from a named failure mode: the prompted system fails a specific, measured way, and the failure persists after reasonable prompt and retrieval work.

topics.label: The full cost of a tune
topics.detail: Estimate the full cost before starting, including data creation, training runs, evaluation, serving the tuned model, and retraining when the base model is replaced.

topics.label: Tied to one base model
topics.detail: Understand that a fine-tune ties you to one base model version, so a better base model next quarter means repeating the work rather than changing a model name.

modules.outcome: Decide whether a task justifies fine-tuning, and state the failure it fixes, the metric that will prove it, and what the tune will cost to own.

modules.title: Data curation for fine-tuning

topics.label: Specify the behavior first
topics.detail: Define the behavior you want in writing before collecting data, so every example can be checked against the same specification.

topics.label: Where examples come from
topics.detail: Source examples from real usage logs, expert-written demonstrations, or carefully filtered synthetic data, and understand the bias each source brings.

topics.label: Match the chat template
topics.detail: Format examples in the chat template the base model was trained with, since a mismatched template silently degrades the tune and the model that serves it.

topics.label: Loss on responses, not prompts
topics.detail: Decide what the model should learn from each example, and mask the loss so training targets the assistant's responses rather than the prompts.

topics.label: Few clean beats many noisy
topics.detail: Understand why a few hundred clean, representative examples often beat thousands of noisy ones for a narrow task.

topics.label: Cleaning bad examples
topics.detail: Remove duplicates, contradictions, wrong labels, truncated responses, and synthetic examples that repeat the same phrasing.

topics.label: Balancing edge cases
topics.detail: Balance common cases with the difficult and important edge cases, so the model does not learn that the easy path is always right.

topics.label: Leak-free splits
topics.detail: Split data into training, validation, and held-out test sets, and keep near-duplicates from leaking across the split.

topics.label: PII & licensed content
topics.detail: Check the data for personal information, licensed content, and anything you would not want a model to repeat word for word.

topics.label: Versioning the dataset
topics.detail: Version the dataset alongside the training configuration, so every tuned model can be traced back to exactly what it learned from.

modules.outcome: Produce a clean, versioned, correctly formatted dataset with a held-out test set that can support an honest before-and-after comparison.

modules.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)

topics.label: What SFT changes
topics.detail: Understand how supervised fine-tuning nudges a pretrained or instruction-tuned model toward labelled examples by minimizing loss on the target responses.

topics.label: Hyperparameters that matter
topics.detail: Learn the hyperparameters that matter first: learning rate, epochs, batch size, sequence length, and gradient accumulation.

topics.label: Full vs parameter-efficient
topics.detail: Understand full fine-tuning versus parameter-efficient methods, and why updating every weight is rarely necessary for a narrow task.

topics.label: A first SFT run with TRL
topics.detail: Run a small SFT job with a library such as TRL and confirm that the loss falls on both training and validation data.

topics.label: Reading the loss curves
topics.detail: Read training and validation curves to recognize underfitting, overfitting, and an unstable run that needs a lower learning rate.

topics.label: Catastrophic forgetting
topics.detail: Recognize catastrophic forgetting, where the model gains the narrow skill and loses general abilities it had before.

topics.label: Read outputs, not just loss
topics.detail: Inspect sample outputs at each checkpoint rather than trusting the loss curve alone, since a lower loss does not guarantee better answers.

topics.label: Choosing a checkpoint
topics.detail: Choose the checkpoint to keep from validation behavior, not from whichever epoch happened to finish last.

modules.outcome: Run a supervised fine-tune, read its training curves, and pick a checkpoint you can defend.

modules.title: LoRA & QLoRA

topics.label: LoRA adapters
topics.detail: Understand LoRA as freezing the base model and training small low-rank adapter matrices that are added to selected layers.

topics.label: QLoRA on a quantized base
topics.detail: Understand QLoRA as loading the frozen base model in quantized form so the same tune fits on a much smaller GPU.

topics.label: Rank, alpha & target modules
topics.detail: Reason about the settings that matter: rank, alpha, target modules, dropout, precision, and quantization type.

topics.label: Adapters vs full fine-tuning
topics.detail: Understand the trade-off between adapter-based tuning and full-model fine-tuning on quality, memory, training time, and storage.

topics.label: PEFT with Unsloth or Axolotl
topics.detail: Fine-tune an open-weight model with PEFT through tooling such as Unsloth or Axolotl, using a configuration file you can rerun exactly.

topics.label: Estimating GPU memory
topics.detail: Estimate GPU memory from parameter count, precision, sequence length, and batch size before renting hardware.

topics.label: Tracking runs
topics.detail: Track each run with its dataset version, configuration, and evaluation results so experiments can be compared rather than remembered.

topics.label: DIY vs managed fine-tuning
topics.detail: Compare running the tune yourself with a managed fine-tuning service, including which base models it offers and whether you can take the weights away.

modules.outcome: Fine-tune an open-weight model efficiently on a single GPU, with a configuration and results another engineer can reproduce.

modules.title: Preference tuning & DPO

topics.label: Demonstrations vs preferences
topics.detail: Understand the difference between demonstration data, which shows one correct answer, and preference data, which says that one answer is better than another.

topics.label: Building preference pairs
topics.detail: Create preference examples containing a prompt, a preferred response, and a rejected response that differ in the quality you care about.

topics.label: Sources & rater agreement
topics.detail: Collect preferences from human raters, from your own eval judges, or from production feedback, and check how often raters agree with each other.

topics.label: Avoiding length bias
topics.detail: Avoid preference pairs that differ in irrelevant ways, such as length, which teach the model the wrong lesson.

topics.label: DPO intuition
topics.detail: Understand the intuition behind Direct Preference Optimization without reinforcement-learning mathematics: raise the likelihood of preferred answers relative to rejected ones.

topics.label: DPO after SFT
topics.detail: Run DPO on top of an SFT checkpoint, and understand why preference tuning usually follows supervised tuning rather than replacing it.

topics.label: What preference tuning is for
topics.detail: Use preference tuning for qualities that are hard to write as a single correct answer, such as tone, helpfulness, refusal behavior, or concision.

topics.label: When SFT is enough
topics.detail: Know when SFT alone is sufficient and when preference optimization adds measurable value.

modules.outcome: Use preference data when the desired behavior is better expressed as "A is better than B", and show that it moved the metric you targeted.

modules.title: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT)

topics.label: Reward-based tuning
topics.detail: Understand reward-based fine-tuning, where the model's outputs are scored and training pushes it toward higher-scoring behavior.

topics.label: RFT vs SFT vs DPO
topics.detail: Distinguish RFT from SFT and preference optimization by what each one learns from: examples, comparisons, or a reward.

topics.label: Tasks with gradable outputs
topics.detail: Identify tasks suited to RFT, where outputs can be graded reliably and automatically, such as code that must pass tests, math with checkable answers, or structured outputs with verifiable fields.

topics.label: Reward design & reward hacking
topics.detail: Understand reward design as the hard part, and recognize reward hacking, where the model optimizes the grader instead of the real objective.

topics.label: Reaching RFT in practice
topics.detail: Understand why RFT is usually reached through a managed service or a specialized framework rather than built from scratch.

modules.outcome: Recognize when reward-based tuning is justified and write a grader that rewards the behavior you actually want.

modules.title: Distillation

topics.label: Teacher → student
topics.detail: Understand teacher-to-student distillation: a stronger model produces outputs that train a smaller model for one narrow workload.

topics.label: Generating & filtering teacher outputs
topics.detail: Generate teacher outputs on inputs that resemble real traffic, and filter them with your evals before they become training data.

topics.label: Capability for cost & latency
topics.detail: Use distillation to trade a small amount of capability for lower cost, lower latency, and a model you can host yourself.

topics.label: Copied mistakes, low diversity
topics.detail: Understand the risks of copying teacher mistakes and of low-diversity synthetic data that narrows what the student can handle.

topics.label: Teacher terms of use
topics.detail: Check the teacher model's terms of use, since some providers restrict using their outputs to train competing models.

modules.outcome: Specialize a smaller model to approximate a stronger one on a specific task, with the capability given up and the cost saved both measured.

modules.title: Evaluating fine-tunes

topics.label: Baselines before training
topics.detail: Establish the baselines before training: the base model, the best prompted version of it, and a stronger model with the same prompt.

topics.label: Same held-out set, same judge
topics.detail: Evaluate every candidate on the same held-out test set with the Level 7 evaluation framework, using the same metrics and the same judge.

topics.label: Beyond a single score
topics.detail: Compare quality, latency, cost per request, output consistency, and specific failure cases rather than a single aggregate score.

topics.label: Regressions outside the task
topics.detail: Check for regressions outside the narrow capability you tuned, including general instruction-following, safety behavior, and formats the tune never saw.

topics.label: Reading individual failures
topics.detail: Read individual failures from the tuned model, since an average improvement can hide a new failure the base model never had.

topics.label: Simpler alternatives, one last time
topics.detail: Compare against simpler alternatives one final time, and accept the result when a better prompt or a stronger base model wins.

topics.label: Writing the decision down
topics.detail: Write the decision down: what improved, by how much, what regressed, and whether the gain justifies serving and maintaining the tune.

modules.outcome: Demonstrate that a fine-tune provides measurable value on the target task without unacceptable regressions elsewhere, or show convincingly that it does not.

modules.title: Serving the adapter

topics.label: Separate adapter or merged weights
topics.detail: Choose between keeping a LoRA adapter separate from the base model and merging it into the weights, and understand what each choice means for storage, loading, and swapping.

topics.label: Save, load & merge
topics.detail: Save, load, and merge adapters, and confirm that the merged model reproduces the adapter's evaluation results.

topics.label: Multi-LoRA serving with vLLM
topics.detail: Serve the base model with one or several adapters through vLLM, where many adapters can share one base model on the same GPU.

topics.label: Quantized export for Ollama
topics.detail: Export the tuned model to a quantized format for local runtimes such as Ollama, and re-run evaluation after quantization, since it can undo part of the gain.

topics.label: Managed & serverless adapter hosting
topics.detail: Host an adapter on a managed platform or a serverless inference provider that serves adapters on shared base models, and compare that with running your own GPU.

topics.label: Matching template & tokenizer
topics.detail: Serve with exactly the chat template and tokenizer used in training, since a template mismatch is the most common reason a good tune behaves badly in production.

topics.label: Versioning & rollback
topics.detail: Version the adapter, base model, dataset, and configuration together, and keep the previous version deployable for rollback.

topics.label: Gradual rollout via the gateway
topics.detail: Route traffic between the base model and the tuned model through your gateway, and roll the tune out gradually while watching evaluation and production metrics.

topics.label: Latency & cost vs baseline
topics.detail: Measure latency and cost per request for the served tune and compare them with the prompted baseline the tune replaced.

topics.label: Retraining triggers
topics.detail: Plan for retraining: decide what triggers it, such as a new base model, drifting inputs, or new failure cases, and how the eval suite gates each new version.

modules.outcome: Deploy a fine-tuned model behind your existing gateway with versioning, rollback, and measured latency and cost, and know when it needs retraining.

modules.title: Capstone: a LoRA that beats a prompted baseline

projects.title: Capstone: a LoRA that beats a prompted baseline
projects.result: a served fine-tuned model that beats a strong prompted baseline on a stated metric, with the evaluation numbers, the regressions checked, and the cost of owning it written down.

checklist.label: A narrow task with a measured failure
checklist.detail: Choose one narrow, real task where the best prompt you can write still fails in a way you can measure.

checklist.label: Metric & threshold up front
checklist.detail: Write down the failure, the metric that will judge success, and the threshold the tune must clear before any training starts.

checklist.label: A strong prompted baseline
checklist.detail: Build the strongest prompted baseline you can, including few-shot examples and retrieval where relevant, and record its score on a held-out test set.

checklist.label: Clean, leak-free dataset
checklist.detail: Create a clean, versioned dataset with training, validation, and held-out splits that do not leak into each other.

checklist.label: Reproducible LoRA/QLoRA run
checklist.detail: Run an SFT tune with LoRA or QLoRA from a configuration file someone else can rerun, and add preference tuning only if the evaluation shows a gap it can close.

checklist.label: Same-set comparison & cost
checklist.detail: Evaluate the tuned and prompted models on the same held-out set, and report quality, latency, tokens per request, and cost per thousand requests.

checklist.label: Regressions & one failure
checklist.detail: Test for regressions on prompts outside the target task, and document at least one failure the tune introduced or failed to fix.

checklist.label: Serve it, reproduce the numbers
checklist.detail: Serve the adapter behind an endpoint with the correct chat template, and confirm the served model reproduces the offline evaluation numbers.

checklist.label: A fine-tuning decision record
checklist.detail: Write a one-page fine-tuning decision record: the failure, the data, the configuration, the before-and-after numbers, the cost to serve, and the retraining trigger.
